constraints: Retries of the same action must not schedule a second portion; a later intentional portion is a separate action.
The control plane owns durable acceptance records; the device executor owns execution and can report an uncertain outcome without automatically dispensing again.
Two concurrent requests for the same action may arrive. Reusing its identity with different action parameters must be rejected.
Polling progress must not trigger dispensing. Acceptance does not mean that a portion has been released.

feedback.details:
The command requests future work; its durable operation record is an addressable resource, and a query reads that record without starting work. The control plane atomically creates one acceptance record keyed by device and action identity, binding the action parameters to it. Concurrent identical requests resolve to that same operation; a different payload under the same identity is rejected as a conflict. A later intentional portion uses a new identity.

Acceptance, delivery and execution are distinct states. The device executor must enforce replay safety at the physical effect boundary and report completion only when established. If it crashes after dispensing but before recording the outcome, a request ID or an HTTP method alone does not establish exactly-once execution: keep the outcome uncertain and reconcile it without an automatic second portion. GET status remains read-only. A PortionDispensed event at acceptance falsely claims a fact, a permanent dispense=true flag cannot distinguish successive portions, and a new identity on every retry turns uncertainty into another action. For an idempotent desired state such as keeping a valve closed, a desired-state resource could instead be appropriate.

messages.text: GET progress may be polled or prefetched; using that read to dispense violates its safe read semantics. The action must be requested separately.
At acceptance the device may still be offline. PortionDispensed would report completion before it exists; an accepted-command message and a completion fact have different meanings.
The unchanged true flag cannot distinguish a second intentional portion from reconciliation of the first. This action needs its own command identity rather than a persistent desired state.
After a lost acceptance response, a new identity represents a new action. Deduplicating each identity does not prevent two portions for the original intention.

feedback.reason: A lost acceptance response leaves the original action pending, not absent. The same command identity must resolve to that action while a separate status read observes it and a completion event reports an established fact.

options.text: Use GET to request dispensing and return a progress resource. Reuse the URL on retry, and let the device publish completion after dispensing.
Publish PortionDispensed when the control plane accepts the request. Let the device consume that event, deduplicate its identity, and expose progress through a resource.
Accept a command with a stable action identity, return its status resource, and bind retries to that operation. The device publishes completion only after execution.
Write dispense=true to a desired-state resource and let the device reconcile it. Poll that resource for progress and keep the flag true when requesting another portion.
Accept a command with a fresh action identity for every retry and return its status resource. Let the device deduplicate deliveries independently for each identity.

questions.prompt: A device control plane asks an offline dispenser to release one portion after it reconnects. The caller may retry after losing the acceptance response, and needs to check progress before the device finishes. Which API contract best separates requesting the action, observing its state, and announcing completion?

constraints: The catalog is the authority for asset identity.
A metadata projection may lag by at most 30 seconds.
A missing asset and an unavailable origin are different outcomes.

feedback.details:
Treat `/assets/{assetId}` as the contract boundary, not as a promise that every ingestion path is synchronous. The response can include the metadata projection version or timestamp so callers can apply the stated 30-second limit. A genuine missing asset is a not-found result; an origin failure is an availability error, not a successful empty representation. Starting ingestion from GET would make retries and prefetching trigger work, while exposing table columns would couple clients to persistence details. If callers needed read-your-writes immediately after ingestion, this bounded projection contract would need a stronger completion or version rule.

Boundary and reversal: If the product later requires immediate read-your-writes after ingestion, callers need an accepted-operation or source-version contract in addition to this bounded read.

messages.text: A read now initiates work and conflates a missing asset with an accepted refresh.
Storage schema leaks implementation details and the required outcome distinction is lost.

feedback.reason: The stable asset ID gives callers a durable resource identity, while the projection timestamp makes the 30-second lag interpretable. A read remains a query: it does not start ingestion, and the response distinguishes absence from origin failure.

options.text: Expose a read-only `/assets/{id}` resource with its projection age and distinct not-found and unavailable outcomes.
Treat a missing metadata projection as a refresh request: have the read start ingestion, return pending, and ask callers to poll until it appears.
Expose the catalog table row layout directly and require every caller to infer whether a missing row means no asset or a failed read.

questions.prompt: A media catalog serves metadata for assets. Each asset has a stable asset ID; metadata may lag behind ingestion by up to 30 seconds, and a missing asset must be distinguishable from a failed catalog read. Which contract best fits that read?

constraints: A carrier event has a stable source and event ID across redelivery.
Each shipment has a monotonically increasing revision assigned by the carrier.
The receiver may see events out of order.

feedback.details:
The two identifiers answer different questions. CloudEvents source plus id can identify a repeated event, while the scenario’s carrier revision is an application-level ordering field for one shipment. The event format alone does not guarantee ordered delivery or exactly-once processing. Persist the highest applied revision with shipment state; a duplicate event becomes a no-op, and a lower revision cannot replace a later status. If a carrier cannot provide a monotonic revision, the integration needs a different source-defined ordering rule before claiming that it can reconstruct latest state.

Boundary and reversal: If the carrier guarantees a single ordered stream per shipment and assigns no revisions, the consumer can rely on that explicit contract; no such guarantee is present here.

messages.text: The stated repeated and delayed deliveries violate both assumptions.
Arrival order measures network timing, not the carrier’s state order.

feedback.reason: Event identity handles the same occurrence being redelivered; the carrier revision handles distinct updates arriving out of order. The receiver can therefore suppress duplicates and refuse to move the shipment backward.

options.text: Give each event a stable source/ID and shipment revision; deduplicate repeated IDs and apply only newer revisions.
Rely on the transport to deliver each event once and in order, then overwrite the shipment state with every arrival.
Use receiver arrival time as the revision and overwrite state on each delivery, assuming later received means later occurred.

questions.prompt: A carrier integration emits shipment status changes. Delivery can repeat the same update, and a delayed earlier update may arrive after a newer one. Which event contract lets the logistics service preserve the shipment’s latest state?

constraints: Every document representation carries a strong version validator.
A write based on an older revision must leave the newer document unchanged.
The client can present a conflict and let its user merge.

feedback.details:
An ETag or equivalent strong revision token can be sent as an If-Match precondition. RFC 9110 describes conditional requests as a way to prevent lost updates; the origin evaluates the condition as part of applying the state-changing method. The client can then merge or ask the editor to resolve the conflict. A client-side GET/compare followed by an unconditional write is not atomic, and unconditional replacement makes the stale revision indistinguishable from a current one. If concurrent edits should merge automatically, that is a different domain contract and must define the merge semantics.

Boundary and reversal: If the product later adopts a deterministic merge model, version preconditions may still detect concurrent inputs, but conflict presentation can be replaced by the specified merge behavior.

messages.text: A stale full representation would erase the concurrent edit.
The state can change between the client’s check and its write.

feedback.reason: A server-side precondition closes the race between checking the revision and applying the edit. A mismatch becomes an explicit conflict instead of a lost update.

options.text: Submit the read version as an If-Match precondition; write only if it remains current, otherwise return a conflict.
Replace the document unconditionally with the revision 41 copy, letting the last save win and avoiding a merge response.
Have the client compare a fresh GET locally, then send an unconditional PUT to avoid a conflict response.

questions.prompt: A document editor reads revision 41. Another editor may save revision 42 before the first editor submits its changes. The server must not silently overwrite the intervening edit. Which save contract meets that requirement?

constraints: The available count can change between a browse and a reservation.
Both buyers can submit before either receives a response.
A losing buyer should learn that no reservation was created.

feedback.details:
The command contract names the authoritative outcome: reservation ID on success, or a conflict that does not create a reservation. The state change must enforce `available >= requested` and decrement in the same atomic operation or equivalent serialization boundary. A read followed by a write leaves a race window; a cache is suitable for display only when the scenario permits stale estimates, not for deciding whether the invariant holds. If partial reservations are allowed, the response must state the accepted quantity explicitly rather than imply the full request succeeded.

Boundary and reversal: If inventory is split across independent authorities, a single atomic reserve is unavailable; the product would need to define allocation, compensation and the user-visible partial outcome.

messages.text: Both buyers can read the same final unit before either write occurs.
A later repair does not undo an already accepted oversell.

feedback.reason: The availability query cannot serialize competing buyers. The reserve command must couple the stock check and state change at the authority, and a conflict must mean no reservation was accepted.

options.text: Make the stock check and decrement one atomic reserve command; return a reservation or a conflict with none created.
Read stock first, then submit an unconditional reservation using that count; refresh only if another buyer reports a race.
Accept a cached positive count and let a reconciliation job repair negative inventory after checkout completes.

questions.prompt: An inventory service has exactly one unit left. Two buyers can try to reserve it at the same time; the service must never confirm both reservations. Which API behavior preserves that result?

constraints: Completion is a binary state for each learner and module.
Repeating the same completion request must not add another unit of progress.
The service owns the durable progress record.

feedback.details:
Use a stable resource identity such as learner plus module, and define the operation as setting completion, not adding a count. Repeated submissions then converge on the same durable state without requiring each network attempt to be a new event. An increment endpoint turns a retry into duplicate progress; client-side retry suppression cannot distinguish a lost response from an unapplied request. If the domain later allows multiple separately credited attempts, those attempts need their own identities and rules rather than changing the meaning of completion.

Boundary and reversal: If progress is based on independently graded attempts, represent each attempt as a separately identified record; this question’s one-time module-completion rule would no longer apply.

messages.text: A replay becomes additional progress because the operation is an increment.
The client cannot know whether the server committed before the response was lost.

feedback.reason: A set-to-complete resource models the invariant directly: applying the same request twice leaves the same completion state. The API does not infer that a timeout means the first write failed.

options.text: Address completion by learner and module; set it complete so repeating the same request leaves the stored state unchanged.
Post a progress increment for every accepted delivery and use a client timestamp to identify likely duplicate submissions.
Ask the client to suppress a retry after timeout and assume the server did not commit without an acknowledgment.

questions.prompt: A learner can retry a completion submission after losing the response. Completing one module should remain complete once, even if the same submission reaches the service again. Which contract expresses that state?

constraints: A published price revision is immutable.
A quote remains valid for five minutes and must keep the amount returned when it was created.
A newer revision may become current while an existing quote remains valid.

feedback.details:
Treat product price revisions as immutable facts and the quote as a distinct resource that pins one revision. Its five-minute expiry gives a clear boundary after which checkout may require a new quote. A mutable latest-price lookup is appropriate for discovering today’s price, but not for reinterpreting an existing quote. The client can display the amount, yet the server must resolve and retain the authoritative revision when creating the quote. If prices must become effective immediately even for existing quotes, the scenario’s five-minute validity promise must change.

Boundary and reversal: If the business requires emergency price withdrawal to invalidate open quotes, define an explicit revocation rule and return that outcome rather than silently replacing the pinned amount.

messages.text: The same quote changes meaning during its validity period.
The amount can be stale or altered and is not bound to the catalog revision.

feedback.reason: The quote must retain the exact immutable revision that produced its amount. Looking up “current price” again would change a still-valid quote; accepting an unverified client amount would detach the purchase from catalog authority.

options.text: Create an immutable quote bound to one price revision; reads retain its amount until the quote expires.
Resolve the product’s latest price each time the quote URL is read, even if the customer already received an earlier amount.
Have the client send its displayed amount at purchase time and accept it without validating the referenced revision.

questions.prompt: A catalog operator publishes price revisions while checkout requests are in flight. A quote may be retried for five minutes, and the customer must see the same quoted amount throughout that interval. Which contract should checkout use?

constraints: The API promises that a token is rejected for protected requests after revocation succeeds.
The server makes the authorization decision for each protected request.
A client may still hold a copied token after the revocation response.

feedback.details:
Model revocation as a state-changing command with an explicit completion point. The identity service records the revocation and only then returns success; every later protected request consults authorization state that reflects that completion. The implementation may use an epoch, status record, or another durable mechanism, but it cannot acknowledge success while copied tokens remain accepted. If immediate enforcement is unavailable, return a distinct pending outcome or change the promise. Deleting a token from one device does not invalidate copies held elsewhere.

Boundary and reversal: If the product permits a measured revocation delay, the response can state that weaker bound and the checks can enforce it; immediate post-success rejection is the premise here.

messages.text: A request can still be authorized after the API has promised revocation.
A copied or offline token remains usable because the server does not enforce revocation.

feedback.reason: The service must make the revoked state effective for protected requests before it reports success. A queued eventual update or client-only logout leaves copied credentials usable after the promised boundary.

options.text: Persist a new credential epoch before success; protected requests compare the token against the current epoch.
Return success when a revocation message is queued, then let authorization nodes update from the message later.
Tell the active client to delete its token, while server checks continue to accept any otherwise valid copy.

questions.prompt: An identity service revokes a credential. The API promises that once revocation returns success, requests using that credential are rejected; authorization decisions are made by the service, not by offline clients.

constraints: The caller’s 300 ms wait bound is explicit.
A late route preview has no durable value.
The server can observe cancellation or deadline expiry.

feedback.details:
The client deadline expresses how long it is willing to wait; downstream calls should receive the remaining budget rather than reset a fresh timeout at each hop. When the deadline expires, the server should cancel work it spawned where possible. This does not guarantee that every computation can stop instantly, so resource limits still matter. A durable operation resource is useful when work must continue after the caller disconnects; the scenario explicitly says previews are discarded, so that contract would preserve unwanted work.

Boundary and reversal: If dispatchers need to retrieve the route after leaving the screen, the result becomes durable work and should use an explicit operation resource with its own lifecycle.

messages.text: Server and downstream work continue after the only consumer has gone away.
Durable work adds state and retries for a result the scenario does not need to retain.

feedback.reason: A propagated deadline makes the 300 ms budget meaningful across the call chain. Because a late preview has no durable value, cancellation is preferable to persisting work and polling for it.

options.text: Set a realistic request deadline, propagate its remaining budget to downstream calls, and cancel computation when the request expires.
Leave the request open until route computation eventually finishes and let the client abandon the response locally.
Persist every preview as a long-running job and require polling even though late results are discarded.

questions.prompt: A dispatch screen requests a route preview and waits at most 300 ms. A route calculation can exceed that bound, and the result is discarded if it arrives after the screen moves on. Which request contract controls wasted work?

constraints: The decision is evaluated for one authenticated account and one feature key.
Operations can revise the assignment rule without releasing a new app.
Clients need a stable decision and the rule revision used for it.

feedback.details:
Treat evaluation as a query over the authenticated account, feature key and server-owned rule revision. The response carries the evaluated result and revision; the client does not independently reproduce the rollout rule. Shipping percentages and bucketing code lets old clients continue using stale logic after operations changes the rule, while random local assignment is not account-stable. This contract does not promise that every device sees a new decision instantly; any decision-cache lifetime must be specified separately if required.

Boundary and reversal: If the rollout rule becomes a public, immutable client-side configuration and all active clients can update together, distributing it can be appropriate; neither condition holds in this scenario.

messages.text: Old clients can retain obsolete rules, so one account may receive inconsistent decisions during rollout.
The result is not tied to the account or the service’s current assignment rule.

feedback.reason: Clients need an account-specific evaluated decision, not the changing rule implementation. Returning the rule revision makes the decision interpretable while keeping assignment consistent across app versions.

options.text: Evaluate the account against the current server rule and return the decision with its rule revision.
Return the rollout percentages and bucketing algorithm; have every app version calculate the account decision locally.
Let each app choose and cache a random local result until the next release.

questions.prompt: A feature rollout assigns accounts by a rule that operations may revise during the release. Old and new app versions call the same evaluation endpoint; each needs the result for the signed-in account, while the assignment rule itself is maintained by the service.

constraints: Clients can send timestamps with an explicit UTC offset.
Adjacent searches must cover every slot start once, with a boundary-start slot in the later range.
The repeated local hour during a daylight-saving fall-back names two possible instants.

feedback.details:
Normalize query bounds to instants using the explicit offset supplied by the caller. A half-open range includes its start and excludes its end, so a slot on a shared endpoint appears only in the next adjacent query. Offset-free local time can be ambiguous during the daylight-saving fall-back hour; rejecting it unless the caller supplies the intended offset avoids choosing an instant silently. If the business defines a different boundary convention, it must be used consistently by storage, search and clients.

Boundary and reversal: If the product wants end-inclusive ranges, callers must advance the next range past the prior endpoint and the contract must state that behavior; the adjacent-slot premise favors half-open ranges.

messages.text: The same request can identify different instants across servers or daylight-saving transitions.
A slot ending at 10:15 and the next beginning at 10:15 both match the shared boundary.

feedback.reason: Explicit offsets identify instants even when local civil time repeats during daylight-saving fall-back. A half-open range includes its start and excludes its end, so a slot on a shared endpoint appears only once across adjacent queries.

options.text: Normalize explicit-offset timestamps to instants and include the start while excluding the end.
Accept local wall-clock times and use the server’s configured zone to choose an instant for each query.
Include both endpoints and return slots touching a range boundary, then deduplicate the results in the client.

questions.prompt: A scheduling client partitions a date range into adjacent appointment searches. A slot starting exactly at a shared boundary belongs to the later search, and clients may query during a daylight-saving fall-back.

constraints: The index can change between page requests.
The API can retain a snapshot token for the cursor lifetime.
The query and sort order are part of the pagination identity.

feedback.details:
The cursor is a continuation contract, not just an encoded row number. It should bind the normalized filter, sort keys and an index snapshot or equivalent stable boundary; it can expire with an explicit restart response. A live offset is simpler when the collection is static, but this index changes during traversal. Deduplicating IDs only removes repeated rows and cannot reveal an item skipped when earlier rows moved. If the product accepts a live, best-effort feed instead of a stable traversal, its cursor semantics should say so.

Boundary and reversal: If the index cannot retain snapshots, use a stable keyset cursor over a monotonic ordering field and document which concurrent inserts may be excluded.

messages.text: Insertions or removals before the offset can shift results and cause gaps or duplicates.
Deduplication can hide duplicates but cannot recover omitted results or establish a stable view.

feedback.reason: A snapshot-bound cursor holds the query and ordering stable across page requests. Offsets into a changing index can shift, and client deduplication cannot restore omitted records.

options.text: Bind the opaque cursor to the query, sort order and retained index snapshot; require it on the next-page request.
Use a numeric offset against the live index and rebuild ordering for each page, accepting shifts as records arrive.
Return pages without a snapshot and ask each client to remove repeated IDs after it finishes traversing them.

questions.prompt: A discovery API returns large search results in pages. New records and index updates can occur while a user follows the next-page link. The client expects a stable traversal for the same search request.

constraints: The total service can run six solves concurrently.
Each tenant has a separate limit of three in-flight solves.
The client can retry after a capacity rejection.

feedback.details:
Admission needs both the aggregate six-solve ceiling and each tenant’s three-solve ceiling. A tenant-scoped counter enforces the latter while shared capacity enforces the former. Excess work is rejected rather than represented as queued; a retry hint can tell clients when to try again. A global-only cap of three would reject work even when the remaining capacity is available to another tenant. No additional fairness or priority policy is implied.

Boundary and reversal: If callers require eventual execution instead of retrying, change the contract to an explicitly bounded queue with an operation resource and queue-capacity outcome.

messages.text: This moves overload into retained work and violates the explicit no-unbounded-waiting constraint.
One tenant could take four slots, exceeding its stated limit while service capacity remains available.

feedback.reason: A per-tenant in-flight limit enforces the stated admission rule. Excess work must be rejected rather than represented as accepted background work, and a retry hint tells callers when to try again.

options.text: Admit three concurrent solves per tenant; reject excess requests with a capacity status and retry delay, without queueing them.
Accept every request into a queue and retain excess solve inputs until workers catch up.
Limit only the whole service to six concurrent solves, with no per-tenant counter.

questions.prompt: A route-planning service has capacity for six solves. Two tenants may each use three at once, but no tenant may exceed three; excess requests are not queued.

constraints: The issuer decline is a final known result.
Capacity rejection means the authorization was not submitted to the issuer.
Human-readable text may be localized and can change.

feedback.details:
RFC 9457 defines a problem-details format for machine-readable HTTP error details, including a problem type identifier and occurrence-specific explanation. Keep the issuer decline definitive, identify a malformed request as client-correctable, and make the service’s capacity rejection distinct from an issuer result. A Retry-After hint belongs only where the service actually expects a later retry. Detail text helps a person but should not be a protocol field clients parse. If an authorization can have an unknown external outcome, that requires a separate operation/reconciliation contract; this scenario deliberately excludes that condition.

Boundary and reversal: If the processor later adds a timeout with unknown charge outcome, do not map it into these three types; add an explicit unresolved outcome and reconciliation path.

messages.text: Localized or revised prose is not a stable machine contract.
Generic HTTP consumers cannot distinguish a failed authorization from a successful response.

feedback.reason: Stable problem types let callers distinguish correction, final decline, and retryable capacity rejection without parsing text. The HTTP status still communicates the general response class.

options.text: Use HTTP status plus a stable Problem Details type for invalid input, decline and capacity; add retry guidance only for capacity.
Put the category in explanatory prose and ask clients to match words such as “declined” or “busy” in that text.
Return the same success status for all three outcomes and encode the result only in a human-readable response message.

questions.prompt: A payment authorization API can reject a malformed amount, receive a definitive issuer decline, or refuse work because its own capacity limit is reached. Clients must correct, stop, or retry differently for those three outcomes.

constraints: Old workers ignore unknown response fields.
The existing `status` values retain their meanings.
The new field is informative and not required for existing case handling.

feedback.details:
Compatibility must hold in both directions for the deployed readers and writers. Old workers can ignore a new optional field; they cannot safely reinterpret an existing status value that has acquired a second meaning. Keeping the field optional also means an older producer can still send a valid case while deployment rolls forward. A coordinated breaking migration is possible only if the system can actually cut over together, which the scenario rules out. If the reason changes authorization or routing, it is no longer merely informative and needs its own compatibility treatment.

Boundary and reversal: If every consumer can be drained and upgraded before the new field becomes required, a versioned breaking change becomes feasible; the several-day coexistence premise rules that out.

messages.text: Existing consumers may misread a value whose meaning changed.
The stated mixed-version window makes simultaneous replacement unavailable.

feedback.reason: An optional additive field allows the overlap period without changing the status contract old workers depend on. The new reason remains supplemental rather than a prerequisite for handling the case.

options.text: Add `reviewReason` as optional data and preserve the existing status field and enum values throughout the overlap.
Add the new reason by changing existing status values to encode both state and reason.
Deploy all consumers at once and make `reviewReason` required in the same release.

questions.prompt: A fraud case API is rolling out a new optional `reviewReason` field. Old and new workers will run concurrently for several days, and existing consumers require the current status field and values.

constraints: The export is an audit artifact once approved.
The source can change after export creation.
The applicable payroll-rules revision is identifiable.

feedback.details:
At creation, record the payroll period, the source watermark or equivalent snapshot boundary, and the rules revision. Give the result an export identity and make subsequent retrieval return the same bytes or a clearly versioned derivative. A latest-data query is useful for a new export but cannot reproduce an earlier approval. Local copies may be useful evidence, yet they do not replace the server’s association between approved inputs and generated output. If corrections require a new official export, issue a new export identity and supersede the prior one explicitly.

Boundary and reversal: If audit policy requires a corrected export to replace the approved one, represent that as a new revision with a link to the superseded artifact.

messages.text: A retry can return a different artifact for the same apparent export identity.
This provides no durable server-side identity or audit link to the approved result.

feedback.reason: The approved export must be an immutable resource tied to its input boundary and rules revision. A later retry retrieves the artifact instead of silently recalculating a different one.

options.text: Create an immutable export resource pinned to period, source watermark and rules revision; retrieval returns that artifact.
Make the same period URL recalculate from current rows and current rules on every GET.
Ask finance to save the first file locally and treat later server output as an unrelated export.

questions.prompt: A finance operator reruns a payroll export after a network failure. Source records may be corrected later, and tax rules can be revised; an audit must reproduce the same export that was approved originally.

feedback.details: Treat revocation as an authorization-state transition, not just an HTTP request being accepted. The identity authority advances a credential or session epoch (or marks the credential revoked), and each server-side check compares the session’s recorded epoch/status with the current value. The endpoint may return success only once the checks that protect requests enforce that value. If propagation is still pending, report pending/unavailable and fail closed at the affected boundary. Short token lifetime and refresh-token revocation reduce future exposure, but neither invalidates an already-issued access token immediately.

messages.text: A 30-minute residual lifetime means an old session remains usable after the endpoint reports success; expiry alone does not meet immediate revocation semantics.
Blocking refresh prevents renewal but leaves already-issued access tokens usable until expiry.
The queue write does not show that authorization checks enforce the revocation; a gateway that has not consumed the event still accepts the old session.
A client can be offline or malicious and cannot revoke a bearer credential at the server-side authorization boundary.

feedback.reason: A successful revocation must change the rule used by the authorization enforcement point. Checking a current credential/session epoch makes each new authorization decision reject sessions issued under the prior epoch; a queued notification or client-side cleanup is only propagation work.

options.text: Advance the credential epoch and require authorization checks to enforce it before returning success.
Stop issuing tokens and document the remaining 30-minute validity window for existing access tokens; let them expire naturally before treating all sessions as revoked.
Revoke refresh tokens and keep validating existing access tokens locally until they expire; force users to authenticate again only on their next refresh.
Write a revocation event to a queue, return success immediately, and allow gateways to keep accepting old sessions until they consume it.
Return success after asking the client to clear its local session, while the server continues validating previously issued tokens.

questions.prompt: After an administrator revokes a credential, the revocation endpoint returns success. Some access tokens issued before the revocation may remain unexpired for 30 minutes. What must the identity service guarantee before it reports revocation as successful?

feedback.details: The HTTP response should acknowledge only a durable job record, typically with an operation ID and Location for a status resource. Persist the client intent and job state before returning 202; use the same client idempotency identity to resolve a lost response to the same job, and reject reuse with different parameters. A worker lease lets another worker resume after a crash. The request ACK does not claim the rendition is complete. GET reads the recorded job state and never schedules work. A long unary request can time out while processing continues, while an in-memory queue loses acknowledged work on process death.

messages.text: The 20-minute operation exceeds the caller’s 200 ms budget; a timed-out request does not reveal whether the original work continues, and a fresh submission can duplicate it.
A crash between the early response and durable persistence loses work that the service already claimed to accept.
A process-local queue cannot recover an acknowledged job after that process disappears; polling cannot reconstruct missing durable intent.
Status reads may be retried, cached, or prefetched; making GET start work violates safe read semantics and can create duplicate execution.

feedback.reason: Acceptance and completion are separate states. A stable operation identity and durable job record make the acknowledgement recoverable; the worker lease recovers execution, and a read-only job resource reports progress without creating another job.

options.text: Create a durable job ID at acceptance and expose status and result through that resource.
Hold the request open through all rendition work; if its 200 ms caller deadline expires, ask the caller to submit a new job with a fresh request identity.
Return 202 when a process-local worker receives the request, then persist job state after the worker starts; retry a lost response by submitting again.
Put the job only in a process-local queue and return its ID; if the worker process dies, recreate the job from the client’s next poll.
Return a job URL whose GET handler starts or restarts transcoding whenever the caller polls for status.

questions.prompt: A video service accepts a transcoding request and returns within 200 ms. The worker may crash immediately after acceptance, and the job can run for 20 minutes. What HTTP resource contract lets the caller retry safely and lets the system recover the work?

feedback.details: Treat the feature decision and persisted-data migration as separate changes. For this week of mixed app versions, the new field must be optional or have an old-reader-safe default, and both versions must read records written by the other. If writers populate both representations, define which one is authoritative and how conflicts are resolved. Turning the flag off must not require reversing an incompatible data rewrite. Only after old readers have been retired and rollback is no longer required should a later migration remove the old representation.

messages.text: A flag rollback does not reverse an in-place data rewrite; old app versions can no longer read records changed to the incompatible shape.
A stale client flag cannot restore server-side compatibility for persisted records or guarantee that old readers see a safe representation.
The stated one-week coexistence means old clients remain active; requiring simultaneous deployment violates that constraint and leaves no safe rollback path.
Dual writes alone do not define which representation readers trust or whether a rollback preserves the old reader’s interpretation.

feedback.reason: A feature flag controls exposure, while data compatibility controls whether old and new readers can operate during rollback. An additive, dual-readable shape preserves the old contract until the rollback window closes; destructive cleanup is a later, separately gated step.

options.text: Expand readers and writers compatibly before rollout; keep the data change reversible through the coexistence window.
Rewrite persisted records into the new shape before enabling the flag, then rely on turning the feature flag off to restore the old behavior.
Ship the new write format and keep rollback solely in a client-side flag cache that may remain stale after the server turns the feature off.
Make the new field mandatory in one coordinated release and require all clients to upgrade before serving requests.
Write both old and new fields during rollout but leave reader precedence and rollback interpretation unspecified; remove either field when the first new client launches.

questions.prompt: A feature rollout must be reversible within five minutes while old and new app versions coexist for a week. Old readers ignore unknown optional fields; new readers safely default the new field when it is absent. What data-evolution contract keeps rollback safe?

feedback.details: Two buyers with distinct idempotency keys are not duplicate requests. Each can pass an earlier availability read, so neither a request key nor a read-then-write flow serializes the resource-wide rule. Put the overlap check at the reservation owner’s commit boundary: one transaction succeeds, and the other receives a conflict (or an explicit pending result until the same atomic claim resolves). A database exclusion constraint or a serializable transaction can enforce the invariant; an in-process lock works only if it truly covers every writer, which the multi-instance API does not. Never send confirmation before the authoritative claim commits.

messages.text: Idempotency prevents replay of one intent; the two valid keys represent different intents, so it does not prevent their ranges from overlapping.
Both requests can observe the same free state before either writes. Without an atomic check-and-reserve, both unconditional inserts can succeed.
Separate API instances have separate mutexes, so concurrent requests routed to different instances do not share the exclusion rule.
A later cancellation cannot make the original double confirmation true; users may already have relied on both bookings.

feedback.reason: Idempotency is scoped to one intent. The invariant spans all intents competing for one resource, so the authoritative write must atomically reject any time range that overlaps an existing reservation.

options.text: Enforce non-overlap atomically at the booking authority, independent of each request’s idempotency key.
Deduplicate identical retries by key, but allow each distinct key to insert its own reservation after the availability read.
Read the available slots, confirm both requests saw the slot as free, then insert each booking without a conditional write or exclusion check.
Protect the booking check with an in-process mutex on each API instance, while allowing requests to reach different instances.
Confirm both bookings immediately and run a background conflict resolver that cancels one booking later.

questions.prompt: Two buyers simultaneously request overlapping appointment ranges for the same resource. Each request has a different valid idempotency key, and both availability reads show the slot as free. What must the reservation API enforce so that at most one booking is confirmed?

feedback.details: Keep the source record authoritative. Publish the source checkpoint and the highest contiguous sequence applied by the index, together with the query’s as-of watermark or lag. When a record is newer than the index watermark, return a stale/not-yet-indexed outcome or a bounded-staleness response; reserve not-found for a source-authoritative absence. A received-but-not-applied event is not enough evidence that search includes the record. This contract lets clients retry or explain freshness without silently turning projection lag into data loss.

messages.text: The known source record is committed after the indexed watermark; a 404 without freshness state misreports lag as absence.
A full source scan on every miss is unbounded and still gives the caller no way to assess the projection’s freshness.
A gap between source and index progress indicates work not yet applied, not deletion of authoritative data.
Receiving an event is not the same as applying it; the client needs the indexed/applied watermark to measure actual search freshness.

feedback.reason: The source sequence is 8400 but the searchable projection is applied only through 8360. Returning freshness metadata and an explicit not-yet-indexed state makes that gap observable instead of claiming the source object does not exist.

options.text: Expose the indexed-through watermark and return fresh results only after the query reaches the requested source sequence.
Return the same permanent 404 whenever the current index has no row.
On every index miss, scan the full source store synchronously and omit the index watermark from the response.
Treat the index watermark as the source of truth and mark every record after it as deleted until indexing catches up.
Record the last source sequence received by the indexer, but do not report which sequence has actually been applied to searchable state.

questions.prompt: A media record is committed at source sequence 8400, while search indexing has processed only through 8360. A search for the known record returns no hit. What read contract lets the client distinguish indexing delay from true source absence?

feedback.details: Estimate the resource cost of route recomputations and cap their concurrent and queued work. Preserve a lane or capacity budget for urgent dispatch, and return a clear deferred/rejected result for batch work when its budget is exhausted. A durable queue is useful for accepted batch jobs but does not itself provide latency isolation. Priority metadata also cannot preempt work already occupying all workers. Monitor queue age and urgent deadline misses so the reservation can be adjusted from observed load.

messages.text: A priority label alone does not reserve execution or admission capacity once long-running jobs occupy every worker.
Durability protects queued work from loss but an unbounded backlog can still delay urgent jobs beyond their 100 ms deadline.
Separate worker counts do not isolate the shared bottleneck; batch load can still consume the CPU or dependency urgent routing needs.
Retrying a saturated urgent request adds more work to the constrained path and worsens the deadline miss.

feedback.reason: The two workloads have different deadlines and costs. Bounded weighted admission for batch work plus reserved urgent capacity prevents long recomputations from consuming every resource needed for the 100 ms path.

options.text: Reserve compute capacity for urgent routing so batch recomputation cannot consume its 100 ms budget.
Mark urgent requests as high priority but send urgent and batch work to the same unbounded worker pool.
Accept every batch recomputation into a durable but unbounded queue and let urgent work wait behind existing jobs.
Autoscale batch workers separately while both classes still compete for the same saturated CPU or downstream routing capacity.
Retry urgent route requests whenever they miss 100 ms, without limiting the number of callers or attempts.

questions.prompt: A dispatch service must produce an urgent route within 100 ms. Nonurgent route recomputation can consume several CPU-minutes and may wait for a later batch window. What admission contract prevents batch work from exhausting urgent capacity?

feedback.details: Persist the payment intent before calling the provider and bind the key to immutable request parameters such as amount and currency. Reuse the same provider idempotency key when retrying or querying the result. If the response is lost, expose pending/unknown and reconcile against the provider before changing the state to succeeded or failed. Reject a retry that reuses the identity with different parameters. A new key after timeout is a new financial side effect, and a later refund is weaker than preventing the duplicate in the first place.

messages.text: The provider may already have accepted the first request; a fresh identifier represents another charge rather than a retry of the same intent.
Gateway deduplication cannot prevent a duplicate side effect if each provider request has a new identity.
A response timeout proves only that the result is unknown; reporting final failure invites a second payment while the first may have succeeded.
Post-hoc detection and refund do not prevent the customer from being charged twice or guarantee recovery of the funds.

feedback.reason: A timeout leaves the provider outcome uncertain, not failed. Stable identity and parameter binding make retries refer to the same intended charge; reconciliation must resolve that intent before a new one is created.

options.text: Keep one durable payment intent and reconcile its provider outcome before issuing another charge.
Treat the timeout as a failed charge and submit a new provider request with a fresh charge identifier.
Reuse a client request key at the gateway but send a new provider idempotency key on every provider retry.
Mark the payment failed as soon as the response deadline expires and tell the customer to try again with a new intent.
Create a second charge immediately, then compare provider settlement records later and refund any duplicate.

questions.prompt: A payment provider times out after receiving an authorization request, so the merchant cannot tell whether it charged the customer. What retry contract avoids a second charge while the first outcome is unknown?

feedback.details: Persist the high-risk case and its stable identity before returning accepted. Queue priority and reserved capacity keep low-value volume from consuming all admission slots, while fair scheduling prevents starvation among accepted cases. When the durable queue is full, return an explicit overload/defer response for low-value submissions and do not claim high-risk acceptance unless its record is durable. A priority bit alone is insufficient because it does not create storage or capacity. Track accepted-but-unprocessed age and rejected/deferred counts as overload signals.

messages.text: An in-memory or non-durable broker acknowledgment does not prove the high-risk case survives overload or process loss.
FIFO ordering lets a large low-value backlog occupy admission capacity and delay the high-risk cases the policy must protect.
A metric cannot repair the false acceptance response; an acknowledged case must have a durable record or the API must report defer/reject.
Scheduling priority affects work already admitted; it cannot recover a high-risk case that was never durably recorded.

feedback.reason: The service has two explicit overload classes: accepted high-risk cases must persist, while low-value work may receive a visible defer/reject result. Durable admission before acknowledgment and bounded priority/fairness rules implement that contract.

options.text: Durably admit high-risk cases before acknowledgment and reserve review capacity for them.
Acknowledge high-risk cases when a broker accepts them in memory, then rely on consumers to rebuild any case lost during overload.
Put all risk classes into one FIFO queue and let the earliest low-value backlog consume the capacity needed by new high-risk cases.
Return accepted for every case, then discard low-value or high-risk records if the queue is full and count drops in a metric.
Give high-risk work the highest scheduling priority but acknowledge it before its queue record is durably stored.

questions.prompt: A fraud service has limited review capacity. High-risk cases must never disappear after an acceptance response, while low-value cases may be deferred or rejected during overload. What queue admission policy meets both requirements?

feedback.details: Persist the export request’s period, source cutoff/snapshot identifier, rules revision, and completed artifact under a stable exportId. Once published, treat the bytes and metadata as immutable. A later payroll correction creates a new export identity; it does not rewrite the old export. This makes retries, audits, and downloads reproducible. A GET must only retrieve the artifact and must not silently rerun the calculation against current data.

messages.text: A period URL identifies the subject period but not the approved snapshot; recomputation can return different bytes after the correction.
Overwriting by period erases the originally approved output and makes an old retry silently refer to new data.
Updating inputs changes the meaning of an accepted exportId, so a retry may no longer reproduce the result first approved.
A cache keyed only by period can serve either old or new bytes without identifying which source cutoff and rules produced them.

feedback.reason: The export is a historical artifact. Its identity must pin both the source snapshot and the rules revision; a GET of that immutable identity returns the stored result even after later corrections.

options.text: Pin each download to an immutable export ID, source cutoff, and rules revision.
Use a stable URL such as /exports/2026-09 and regenerate its response from current payroll rows and rules on every GET.
Use the payroll period as the only export identity, overwriting the artifact whenever corrections arrive for that period.
Keep one export job row whose input snapshot and rules revision are updated to the latest values whenever a retry starts.
Cache the latest export response by period and rely on cache expiry to eventually replace it with corrected payroll data.

questions.prompt: A payroll export for period 2026-09 is completed under tax-rules revision 17 and published as a downloadable file. Payroll data is later corrected under revision 18. Which resource contract makes a retry of the original export return the same approved output?

feedback.details: Select a source snapshot or cutoff before reading accounts, invoices, and payments, then calculate every component against that same boundary. Include the period and as-of watermark in the output. If the storage system cannot provide a single snapshot, use a coordinated versioned cutoff and expose the weaker guarantee explicitly; per-table watermarks must not be presented as one coherent snapshot. Updates after the cutoff belong to a later report version.

messages.text: Combining independently current reads can include an invoice without its corresponding payment or balance update and produce totals that never existed together.
A wall-clock label does not make separate reads share a database snapshot; records committed during the run can still produce a mixed view.
Different watermarks explicitly show different source cuts, so the aggregate cannot be interpreted as one consistent report snapshot.
A later correction may be useful, but the original report needs a stable cutoff and a new version if its contents change.

feedback.reason: A multi-table aggregate is meaningful only when its inputs share a declared consistency boundary. One snapshot/cutoff plus a returned watermark makes both the calculation and its freshness auditable.

options.text: Read every report aggregate from one consistent snapshot at the declared cutoff.
Read each table at its latest available state and combine the results, even when each read observes a different commit time.
Label the report with its start time but run ordinary reads over a period while new writes continue to appear.
Return a different watermark for each table and let consumers treat the combined totals as one period-end snapshot.
Publish the mixed-cutoff report as final, then expect a later background reconciliation to update totals without changing the report identity.

questions.prompt: A financial report joins balances from accounts, invoices, and payments for a period ending at 2026-09-30. Updates can arrive while the report is running. What read contract keeps totals internally consistent and lets consumers know what data the report includes?

feedback.details: Set a finite ingest queue or buffer, define whether excess telemetry is delayed or rejected, and communicate that state to producers. Give query serving a protected connection/worker budget so an ingest backlog cannot occupy it. Monitor ingest queue age, dropped/deferred events, and query latency. Durable buffering alone is not isolation if draining still shares the analyst query pool.

messages.text: An unbounded shared pool allows the 40,000-event burst to occupy connections needed to keep queries under 250 ms.
Priority applied after producers take every connection cannot protect the query path; capacity must be reserved at admission.
Silent loss contradicts an explicit overload contract and gives producers no signal to slow down or retry safely.
Durable buffering protects events from loss but a shared drain/query budget still lets ingestion consume interactive capacity.

feedback.reason: The ingest burst and interactive query workload have separate capacity and latency needs. Bounded ingest admission plus an independent query budget prevents producers from consuming every query connection and makes overload visible.

options.text: Bound and isolate telemetry ingestion so analyst queries retain their own capacity.
Let producers and analyst queries share an unbounded connection pool and rely on database autoscaling to absorb bursts.
Keep one shared pool and prioritize query statements after ingest producers have already acquired all connections.
Discard telemetry whenever the database is busy, while returning success to producers and tracking only aggregate event counts.
Persist every burst into an unlimited buffer but give buffer draining and interactive queries the same workers and database connections.

questions.prompt: A telemetry ingest burst reaches 40,000 events per second while analysts continue interactive queries against the same database. Query latency must stay under 250 ms; ingest may be backpressured with a visible overload signal. Which capacity contract isolates the two paths?

feedback.details: Apply an outbound deadline shorter than the gateway’s 500 ms budget, reserve a finite number of in-flight calls for this provider, and bound any queue. When those limits are reached, fail or defer that provider’s request explicitly instead of borrowing every shared worker. A provider-specific circuit breaker can stop repeated calls during a known outage, but it should not trip healthy providers. Retrying is bounded and owned by one layer; it does not replace the deadline or concurrency cap.

messages.text: An 8-second wait exceeds the 500 ms budget and ties up shared workers needed by other providers.
An unbounded queue converts blocked threads into unbounded pending work and does not contain provider-specific resource use.
Immediate unlimited retries multiply load on the slow dependency and can keep all shared workers occupied.
A global breaker couples healthy providers to one dependency’s failure and turns a local slowdown into a broader outage.

feedback.reason: A slow external provider must have its own bounded concurrency and queue plus a deadline that fits the caller budget. Bulkhead isolation contains its saturation so healthy providers keep their capacity.

options.text: Put the slow provider behind a bulkhead and enforce the caller deadline at the gateway.
Allow each request to wait for the provider’s full 8-second response in the common gateway worker pool.
Move calls to an asynchronous queue but allow its pending and in-flight work to grow without per-provider bounds.
Retry provider timeouts immediately in the same shared pool until a notification succeeds.
Use one circuit breaker shared by every provider, so repeated slowness at this provider blocks calls to healthy providers too.

questions.prompt: A notification gateway calls an external provider that sometimes takes 8 seconds, while the gateway’s request deadline is 500 ms. Other providers share the same service. What dependency contract contains the slow provider’s impact?

feedback.details: Bind each record to the authenticated principal and a stable event identity, then persist it with integrity protection before returning success. Corrections are additional attributed events, not edits to the accepted record. Restrict read/write privileges. Preserve the record unchanged for seven years; after that, only the authorized audited purge process may remove it. A memory-buffer ACK does not prove durability, while indefinite retention and unrestricted deletion both violate the stated policy.

messages.text: A mutable row can erase the history of prior actions, so the ledger cannot prove what was originally recorded.
A process failure before the background flush can lose an entry that the API already acknowledged.
A client note is not trustworthy provenance; the authenticated principal must be bound by the append authority.
Immutability applies during the seven-year retention period; unrestricted access/deletion or retaining beyond the declared period without the audited purge violates the policy.

feedback.reason: The append ACK must mean the attributed event is durable and tamper-evident. Access stays restricted, and after seven years removal follows an authorized audited purge rather than a silent edit.

options.text: Persist an attributed, integrity-protected audit append before acknowledgment; permit purge only after seven years.
Store the latest audit action in a mutable row keyed by administrator and allow later updates to correct its text.
Acknowledge the append when a logger accepts it in memory, then flush records to durable storage in the background.
Write all actions under one shared service account and keep the original actor only in an optional client-supplied note.
Keep every immutable record forever and allow unrestricted administrators to read or delete any entry without a retention or purge audit.

questions.prompt: A compliance service appends administrator actions to an audit ledger. Each record must identify its authenticated actor, be tamper-evident and immutable during a seven-year retention period, then be removed only through an authorized, audited purge. What append and retention contract meets this policy?

feedback.details: Persist the highest applied carrier revision alongside each shipment state. In one conditional transaction, accept a new event only if its revision is greater than the stored revision; treat the same event ID as a duplicate and quarantine or ignore a lower revision. If the carrier revision is absent, define another source-backed ordering rule before claiming monotonic state. Arrival time and broker order are transport observations, not substitutes for the business revision.
