Persist the case and stable identity before returning accepted/pending; then a worker may process it later. If persistence or bounded queue capacity is unavailable, do not claim acceptance. The response does not mean the fraud decision is complete. A transient broker handoff or in-memory queue is not enough evidence that the case will survive a restart.

messages.text: A best-effort handoff can disappear after success, violating the explicit durable-acceptance condition.
The caller deadline is for acceptance, not for the later human decision; waiting cannot meet the stated request boundary.
Process loss before the copy loses a case already reported as accepted.
Unbounded admission hides overload rather than applying explicit backpressure and can exhaust storage.

feedback.reason: The 120 ms request cannot wait for human review, but accepted high-risk work must be durable. Return pending only after durable queue admission and make capacity exhaustion explicit.

options.text: Durably enqueue the case before acknowledgment, then return a status ID for later analyst review.
Return success after publishing to a best-effort background channel and assume a consumer will recover dropped cases.
Keep the request open until an analyst completes the review, even when that takes longer than the 120 ms budget.
Acknowledge as soon as the process-local queue accepts the case, then copy it to durable storage when load falls.
Accept every high-risk case into an unlimited queue and never report overload to callers.

questions.prompt: A high-risk fraud case must be reviewed later, but the API has a 120 ms response budget. The caller must not be told “accepted” unless the case survives process loss; queue saturation must be visible. What request boundary fits?

feedback.details: Persist a stable allocation operation before returning pending. The inventory authority owns the atomic seat claim; only its committed result changes the operation to confirmed. A timeout or lost response leaves the same operation pending/unknown until a status read or reconciliation resolves it. Streaming progress may be added for convenience, but it does not replace a durable intent or safe retry identity.

messages.text: The claim may complete after the client deadline, so timeout does not prove it failed and a fresh retry may allocate twice.
Enqueue is acceptance, not reservation; a later rejection would invalidate a ticket already presented as confirmed.
A new identity hides the original uncertain attempt and can claim a second seat.
Disconnect loses the only status channel and cannot establish durable ownership of the allocation attempt.

feedback.reason: The remote claim outlives the client deadline, so acceptance and confirmation must be distinct. A durable intent plus status lets retries resolve the same allocation without asserting success early.

options.text: Create one durable allocation intent and return its ID; resolve the seat asynchronously without resubmitting.
Wait synchronously for the remote inventory claim and treat a 300 ms timeout as a failed allocation.
Return confirmed as soon as the allocation message is enqueued, before the seat authority commits the claim.
Require each client retry to create a new intent so the allocator can restart from the beginning.
Stream allocator progress to the caller without persisting the intent or exposing a resumable status resource.

questions.prompt: Ticket inventory allocation may take several seconds because seats are claimed from a remote authority. The client times out after 300 ms, but it must be able to learn whether its original seat request eventually succeeded. Which boundary is safest?

feedback.details: Authenticate the agent, authorize the tenant/case, then fetch at most 20 deterministically ordered messages in the same request. If the query later grows beyond the response budget, an async export can be introduced with a separately scoped authorization check. Queuing every ordinary read obscures a simple result, while querying before authorization or filtering in the client leaks data.

messages.text: The prompt gives a bounded interactive read that fits its budget; unconditional async work adds unnecessary delay and state.
Authorization after query already crosses the required tenant boundary and may expose protected records to logs or intermediaries.
Unbounded data access violates the requested bounded read and expands both cost and disclosure.
A one-time 80 ms read needs no subscription; the server must authorize the tenant independently of transport.

feedback.reason: The query is short and bounded, so a synchronous page fits the interactive use. Tenant authorization must occur before the data query; async work is justified only by an actual long-running case.

options.text: Return the bounded authorized page synchronously and propagate cancellation when the caller leaves.
Queue each case-history read as a durable job and make the agent poll even when the query normally finishes in 80 ms.
Read the 20 messages first, then check tenant membership before sending the response.
Return all history synchronously and let the client display only its latest 20 messages.
Open a long-lived event stream for a one-time history lookup and use the stream connection as authorization.

questions.prompt: A support agent requests the last 20 messages for a case in their own tenant. The indexed history query completes in 80 ms; the endpoint must deny another tenant before reading its records. Which request boundary is appropriate?

feedback.details: Serve the lookup synchronously and attach an as-of timestamp or age. Return not-found only when the source confirms absence; label a lagging projection stale/not-yet-indexed and report source or projection failure as unavailable. This gives callers an honest result without making GET schedule work. A stream would fit a subscription, which the prompt explicitly excludes.

messages.text: The requested operation is a bounded read, and GET should not create ingestion work as an incidental side effect.
Projection lag is not proof that the authoritative asset is absent.
No subscription is requested; a bounded read needs a response, not a persistent connection.
That response hides a freshness-bound violation and conflates stale data with an available authoritative result.

feedback.reason: One bounded GET meets the stated read workload. Its response semantics—not asynchronous job creation—must distinguish freshness, confirmed absence, and unavailable dependencies.

options.text: Return metadata synchronously with its as-of state; preserve distinct missing and unavailable results.
Make GET enqueue metadata ingestion and immediately return a job-accepted response for every lookup.
Return 404 whenever the projection has no row, even if its watermark is behind recent source writes.
Open a long-lived stream for a single metadata read so later asset updates can be sent if they occur.
Return cached metadata with a normal success status even when the source is unavailable and its age exceeds 20 seconds.

questions.prompt: A media client requests metadata for one asset. The projection may be 20 seconds stale; a confirmed absent asset is 404, while a projection or source outage is 503. The client is not subscribing to changes. What request boundary should serve this read?

feedback.details: Persist the command and stable identity before acknowledging acceptance. Deliver it when the device reconnects, and have the device/effect owner record processed command IDs so duplicate delivery does not repeat the unsafe action. Expose accepted, delivered, executed, and uncertain states distinctly. A transport acknowledgment proves only a message-handling step, not the physical outcome.

messages.text: A six-hour offline interval cannot fit a caller-bound synchronous request.
The device is offline and even delivery would not prove physical execution.
Fresh identities make repeated delivery look like new physical commands and bypass replay protection.
Queue acceptance is pending work, not proof of the physical side effect.

feedback.reason: The device can be unavailable for hours, so caller wait and physical completion are separate. Durable async acceptance survives the offline period; deduplication belongs at the actuation effect owner.

options.text: Durably accept the command while the device is offline and expose delivery/execution status by ID.
Keep the control request open until the device reconnects and physically executes the action.
Send the command over a stream and treat a transport write as proof the device acted.
Issue a fresh command ID on every reconnection attempt so the device can retry the action independently.
Return completed when the durable queue accepts the command, then let device execution happen later.

questions.prompt: A command is accepted while an IoT device is offline and may not reconnect for six hours. The caller needs durable acceptance now and later execution status; replay must not repeat an unsafe physical action. Which boundary fits?

feedback.details: Record the event and stable delivery ID durably before returning accepted. One worker owns up to 8 attempts over 24 hours with exponential backoff; if the partner never acknowledges durable acceptance, preserve the event in a durable dead-letter state and expose it for operator recovery. The receiver acknowledges only after persistence. This is at-least-once delivery within an explicit budget, not infinite retry or silent loss.

messages.text: The 10-second or offline dependency would hold request capacity and exceeds a normal caller-bound interaction.
A failure between response and persistence loses an event the sender promised to deliver.
A retry is the same event; changing its ID defeats receiver deduplication and can repeat the side effect.
Unlimited retries violate the 8-attempt/24-hour budget and can amplify an outage; after the bounded window, the event must remain recoverable in dead letter.

feedback.reason: Durable enqueue preserves the event beyond the initiating request. A bounded retry window contains load, while durable dead-letter and operator recovery prevent unacknowledged accepted work from disappearing.

options.text: Durably enqueue one delivery; use eight attempts over 24 hours, then retain it in a recoverable dead-letter state.
Keep the original request open and retry the partner synchronously until it responds successfully.
Return accepted before the delivery event is durably recorded, then attempt to enqueue it in the background.
Assign a new event identity for every delivery attempt so the receiver can process every message independently.
Let the gateway and worker retry without an attempt budget or backoff while the partner is down.

questions.prompt: A partner endpoint may be unavailable for hours. The sender may make at most 8 attempts over 24 hours; if none is durably acknowledged, the event must remain in a durable dead-letter state for operator recovery. What delivery boundary should the sender use?

feedback.details: The document owner compares expectedRevision with the stored value in the same transaction that writes the content and increments the revision. One update commits; a later write still carrying 12 receives conflict and can reload or merge. An earlier read leaves a race window, and asynchronous work only changes when the conflict becomes visible.

messages.text: The requirement is a direct conflict result for a bounded write; asynchronous acceptance would hide that decision from the caller.
A competing edit can commit between check and write; the precondition must be atomic with the mutation.
This silently discards the first successful edit instead of returning the required stale-version conflict.
Transport order does not make the second client’s revision 12 precondition current.

feedback.reason: The update is bounded and the caller needs an immediate conflict result. A synchronous conditional write makes revision checking atomic with mutation; queuing or transport ordering cannot replace the precondition.

options.text: Use compare-and-swap on expected revision so only one concurrent edit commits.
Queue both edits and return accepted before a worker later decides which version wins.
Read revision 12, check it in application code, then issue an unconditional write in a separate operation.
Accept the second write unconditionally and let the last request received overwrite revision 13.
Send writes over an ordered stream and assume arrival order means both are based on the current revision.

questions.prompt: Two editors submit document writes against revision 12. The first commit should advance to revision 13; the second stale write must receive a conflict. The write transaction completes within 50 ms. What request boundary enforces the rule?

feedback.details: At the inventory owner, atomically require quantity greater than zero and decrement/claim it in the same transaction. Only the winning transaction returns confirmed; the other receives conflict or unavailable. A read before write is advisory, and queue acceptance is not reservation. If the system instead returns pending, it must delay confirmation until that same invariant commits.

messages.text: Confirmation precedes the authoritative claim, so both buyers can be promised the same unit.
Both buyers can read one remaining unit before either insert, then both write successfully.
Unary RPC does not serialize application state transitions or enforce the stock invariant.
Locks and caches are not shared across instances and do not guard the single authoritative stock record.

feedback.reason: Checkout needs a definitive answer and the last unit is contested. Synchronous response is appropriate because the bounded authoritative transaction can return its result; the atomic claim prevents double confirmation.

options.text: Claim stock atomically at the inventory owner before confirming either buyer.
Queue both reservations and immediately confirm each buyer; reconcile the inventory count after the workers run.
Check available quantity in a read, then create the reservation unconditionally based on that value.
Use unary RPC and assume the transport serializes concurrent requests to the inventory service.
Use an in-process lock around each API instance’s local quantity cache, then write reservations independently.

questions.prompt: One stock unit remains and two buyers submit reserve requests concurrently. Each needs a definitive answer before checkout may show confirmation. Which request boundary preserves the inventory invariant?

feedback.details: Bind the submission ID to the learner/module and set completion state rather than adding one on every request. A retry with the same identity returns the existing result; a genuinely new completion identity follows the domain’s separate rule. Keep GET read-only. Neither a stream nor a background job adds value for the short scalar update described.

messages.text: No long-running work is given; queueing introduces delay and state without a reason.
A lost response followed by retry can increment twice because the operation is not idempotent.
The operation is one scalar state change, not a continuous progress feed.
GET is repeatable and may be prefetched; a read must not perform the completion side effect.

feedback.reason: This is a small state-setting operation with immediate visibility. A synchronous idempotent set-state request avoids the cost and delay of an async job while making retries converge.

options.text: Set the learner/module completion idempotently in the synchronous response.
Queue every completion as a background job and require polling even though the scalar update is immediate.
Expose incrementCompletion and ask the client to repeat it until it sees a response.
Keep a stream open for the one completion and treat each replayed message as another progress event.
Make GET mark the module complete when the caller refreshes its progress page.

questions.prompt: A learner completes one module; the completion should be visible in the immediate response. The client can retry after a lost response, but retries must not increment progress again. What boundary fits?

feedback.details: The price owner accepts only a revision greater than the current one and commits before returning success. Checkout must validate the authoritative revision or use a precondition so delayed cache invalidation cannot authorize revision 41. Notifications can accelerate propagation, but publication should not wait for every cache and a stream event is not the commit itself.

messages.text: The success response could precede the state checkout must validate, so revision 41 may still be confirmed.
A delayed old revision can overwrite the new price and violate monotonicity.
The authoritative write is short; tying success to every cache consumer makes publication depend on disconnected readers.
A stream notification may be delayed or missed; checkout must validate current revision at its decision point.

feedback.reason: The write is short and publication success must mean revision 42 is authoritative. A synchronous conditional commit gives that meaning; cache invalidation is separate propagation work.

options.text: Commit the new authoritative price synchronously and publish cache invalidation separately.
Return success after queueing the price update, before the authority has committed revision 42.
Accept any update and let the last message received replace the current price, even if it carries revision 41.
Keep the publish request open until every checkout cache and instance acknowledges invalidation.
Broadcast a stream event and assume every checkout has received revision 42 before it can process a purchase.

questions.prompt: A merchant publishes price revision 42. The authoritative write completes in 40 ms, while cache invalidation may take two seconds. Checkout must never confirm revision 41 after publish success. What request boundary should publication use?

feedback.details: Track the revocation epoch and its enforcement progress. Until every path covered by the contract observes the new epoch, return pending or unavailable and reject requests when state cannot be safely established. Only then report success. Storing a request or queueing invalidation is not the same as enforcement; client cleanup and token expiry do not revoke sessions already held elsewhere.

messages.text: The API would report success while the old credential remains usable, contrary to the stated security guarantee.
The caller cannot know whether revocation is enforced, and propagation failure can leave sessions valid indefinitely.
The guarantee requires stopping old sessions, not merely waiting for their existing lifetime.
Other or offline clients still possess the old session and remain accepted by the server.

feedback.reason: The endpoint’s success has a security meaning: old sessions must already fail at the relevant authorization checks. During propagation it must expose pending/uncertain, not success.

options.text: Report revocation success only after authorization checks enforce it; otherwise return pending.
Return success as soon as the revocation request is stored, although auth nodes may still accept old sessions for two seconds.
Queue invalidation messages and provide no status or indication of which enforcement nodes have applied them.
Do not invalidate auth checks; wait for every old token to reach its natural expiration and then report success.
Return success after instructing the user’s current device to clear its session, without changing server authorization checks.

questions.prompt: Credential revocation must stop old sessions from authorizing new requests. Auth enforcement nodes may take two seconds to observe a new epoch. What should the revocation API return during that propagation window?

feedback.details: Persist the job and ID before returning accepted. Workers hold leases so another worker can resume after replacement, while the job’s lifecycle remains independent of the client’s status request. Expose status by read-only lookup. Cancellation must be an explicit job command with its own semantics; closing a poll should only stop the caller from waiting.

messages.text: The request deadline is far shorter than the workload and should not control accepted job lifetime.
Worker replacement loses work that was already acknowledged.
A disconnected status channel does not imply the user canceled durable work.
Polling cannot recover an operation that was acknowledged but never durably recorded.

feedback.reason: A 25-minute task cannot share the 250 ms request lifetime. Durable acceptance and recoverable worker ownership let it outlive the request and any canceled polling connection.

options.text: Accept a durable transcode job ID within the request deadline and keep processing independent of polling.
Hold the submission RPC open until the 25-minute transcode completes and let its deadline terminate the job.
Return accepted when a worker’s in-memory queue receives the task, then rely on that worker to finish.
Stream progress on the submission connection and terminate the transcode whenever the client disconnects.
Return a job ID before the durable job record is written and reconstruct missing work from client polling.

questions.prompt: A video transcode normally takes 25 minutes; the submission request has a 250 ms deadline. The job must survive worker replacement, and a client canceling its status poll must not cancel accepted work. What boundary should the API expose?

feedback.details: Use a compatible expand-and-contract sequence: introduce an optional field/default and readers that tolerate either shape, then enable the server-evaluated flag. Keep old data semantics available throughout the five-minute rollback window and the week of old-client coexistence. Any destructive cleanup occurs only after the old-reader window closes and has its own migration/rollback plan. Turning a flag off cannot reverse data already rewritten.

messages.text: A flag changes behavior, not persisted bytes; old clients can still fail after rollback.
The async migration can alter data while old readers remain active and is not automatically reversed by disabling the flag.
A stale client-side flag cannot coordinate persisted data shape or protect old readers.
The stated week of coexistence prohibits an all-at-once client cutover.

feedback.reason: Flag evaluation and data migration are different state changes. Rollback is safe only if the persisted representation remains readable by both versions during coexistence.

options.text: Roll back the flag while keeping stored records readable by both app versions.
Assume disabling the feature flag will automatically restore records already rewritten into the new incompatible schema.
Asynchronously rewrite all records to the new format, then enable the feature once the migration queue is empty.
Cache the flag in each client and let clients choose which schema to read without server compatibility guarantees.
Make the new field mandatory in one atomic cutover and require all old clients to stop before enabling the flag.

questions.prompt: A rollout flag can be disabled within five minutes, but app versions coexist for a week and both read persisted records. A new schema field is being introduced. Which synchronous/asynchronous boundary keeps flag rollback from breaking old readers?

feedback.details: Use an exclusion constraint or serializable transaction at the resource owner so only one overlapping reservation commits. Confirm after that commit; the losing request receives conflict. A read-then-write race remains even if each client has an idempotency key, because the two keys represent distinct intents. Async handling would need an explicit pending result and still would require the same final atomic guard.

messages.text: The confirmation precedes the invariant check and can promise two users the same time range.
Concurrent requests can both read the slot as free and then commit overlapping rows.
The keys deduplicate each intent independently and do not enforce a resource-wide conflict rule.
Stream order does not make the database conflict check and reservation atomic across all writers.

feedback.reason: The caller needs a definitive booking decision and the authoritative transaction fits the request. Atomic overlap enforcement at commit ensures no success is returned for a conflicting slot.

options.text: Commit the booking only when an atomic guard proves the resource interval is free.
Queue both requests and return confirmed immediately, then resolve overlap conflicts in a background worker.
Read availability in each request and perform unconditional inserts based on the result.
Use separate stable idempotency keys and assume that prevents two different booking intents from overlapping.
Send both requests over a stream and assume the transport orders them before the database writes.

questions.prompt: Two buyers request overlapping appointment ranges for one resource, and each must know whether the booking succeeded before receiving confirmation. The conflict check and reservation are a short bounded transaction. Which request boundary is correct?

feedback.details: Keep source writes authoritative and update the index in the background. Each query reports the index’s applied watermark or age; when the requested source state is newer than that watermark, report stale/not-yet-indexed rather than permanent absence. A source-confirmed missing record can be 404. Making the whole query asynchronous or pretending the projection is current hides the actual consistency contract.

messages.text: The scenario permits asynchronous indexing and a 15-second lag; coupling all writes to every index is unnecessary and may fail unrelated writes.
A missing projection row during a known lag interval does not prove the source record is absent.
The required read is synchronous; only index maintenance is asynchronous in this scenario.
Without the watermark callers cannot assess whether the index is within the 15-second freshness limit.

feedback.reason: Index maintenance is asynchronous, while a query can return synchronously. A watermark makes the bounded lag observable and preserves the distinction between projection delay and source absence.

options.text: Return search results synchronously with the index watermark; report a lagging index as stale rather than claiming the source record is absent.
Block every source write until all search indexes apply it, then assume a successful write means all queries are current.
Return permanent not-found whenever the synchronous index query has no hit, regardless of its applied watermark.
Queue each search query as a background job even though the API can return the current bounded result immediately.
Expose results without an applied watermark and let callers assume the latest source writes are present.

questions.prompt: Source writes are immediate, but search indexing can lag by 15 seconds. The API must return search results synchronously and distinguish a lagging index from a missing source record. What request boundary should it use?

feedback.details: Return a job identity for accepted batch work, apply CPU/cost limits and fair admission, and defer or reject new batches when the bounded budget is reached. Keep urgent dispatch on a protected short path with reserved workers/capacity. An async queue by itself does not provide isolation if both classes drain through the same pool; priority must be enforced before saturation.

messages.text: Minutes of work can occupy the capacity needed to meet the urgent 100 ms deadline.
Durability prevents loss but shared capacity still lets batch work starve dispatch.
A label cannot help if batch tasks already occupy all workers or the queue is unbounded.
Retries add load to the saturated path and do not isolate the heavy workload.

feedback.reason: The two workloads have different time horizons. Batch work should have durable but bounded async execution, while urgent requests retain an independent capacity budget.

options.text: Reserve urgent routing capacity and admit batch recomputation as durable lower-priority work.
Run batch recomputation synchronously in the same request pool as urgent dispatch until each plan is finished.
Queue batch work durably but drain it through the same unreserved worker pool used by urgent requests.
Add a priority field to requests but provide no reserved capacity or bounded admission.
Retry each delayed urgent route at every timeout while batch saturation remains unchanged.

questions.prompt: Urgent dispatch route choices must return within 100 ms. Batch route recomputation takes minutes and is allowed to wait, but must not consume urgent workers. How should the request boundary handle batch work?

feedback.details: Bind the provider request to a durable payment intent before sending it, and reuse the same idempotency key and parameters for retries or queries. If the response is lost, expose pending/unknown and reconcile the same intent; do not create another charge until the first outcome is known. The caller response reports acceptance, not payment completion. A stream cannot remove the ambiguity of a lost provider response.

messages.text: The provider may have charged before the timeout, so a final failure can prompt a duplicate payment.
Each fresh identity can create another charge; a later refund is not a duplicate-prevention contract.
The client cannot query or safely retry the original operation if the response was lost.
The stream can disconnect during the ambiguous outcome and a reconnect with a new identity risks a second charge.

feedback.reason: The provider can outlive the 300 ms caller budget and time out ambiguously. A durable stable intent lets the API return pending and reconcile one charge rather than asserting failure or starting another.

options.text: Keep the original payment intent pending and reconcile it before any new authorization.
Wait for the provider in the original request and mark the payment failed when 300 ms elapses.
Create a new provider charge identity after each timeout and let reconciliation refund duplicates later.
Queue the provider call and return accepted without storing a stable intent or exposing status.
Keep a stream open until the provider responds and treat a stream reconnect as a new authorization.

questions.prompt: A payment provider may have accepted an authorization even though its response times out. The user-facing request lasts 300 ms; later reconciliation is allowed, but the customer must not be charged twice. What request boundary should the payment service expose?

feedback.details: Bind the cursor to SKU, filters, and a stable sort with a unique tie-breaker. State the freshness boundary so a page is treated as a candidate list. Before confirming a unit, the authoritative inventory transaction rechecks and reserves it atomically. Pagination correctness does not make a stale row a reservation.

messages.text: Storage order is not stable; inserts and ties can shift rows between pages and cause duplicates or omissions.
The read may be stale after another buyer reserves stock; only the write owner can claim it.
The client transfer is unbounded and may disclose or process unrelated inventory.
A cursor must continue the same query; reusing it under different filters can skip or expose rows.

feedback.reason: The list is a bounded read projection, while reservation is a separate write invariant. Deterministic cursor paging makes the candidates navigable but cannot guarantee stock remains available.

options.text: Use a stable SKU-and-unit keyset cursor, then recheck availability before a buyer reserves stock.
Return the first 50 rows by storage order and use an offset for the next page.
Treat every displayed available row as a guaranteed reservation and let checkout commit directly from the search result.
Fetch an unbounded inventory list and filter the requested SKU and availability in the client.
Use an opaque cursor but leave SKU/filter ordering out of its context so it can be reused for other inventory searches.

questions.prompt: The inventory page lists available units by SKU, but another buyer may reserve stock after the page loads. The client needs a bounded, repeatable list; the page itself must not promise availability. Which read contract fits?

feedback.details: Authorize the account before querying. Use completedAt plus itemId as a deterministic order so timestamp ties are resolved, and bind the cursor to learner/filter/snapshot context. Define whether the scan pins a snapshot or allows new items only in a later refresh. Keep write deduplication separate: paging cannot stop a retried completion from incrementing progress.

messages.text: Equal completion times leave records without a total order, so a page boundary can repeat or omit items.
The cursor must be bound to the authorized learner; client filtering does not protect another learner’s data.
A read cursor controls listing order; it does not prevent duplicate progress increments on the write path.
New rows can move offsets and cause duplicates or omissions across the learner’s history.

feedback.reason: Stable history requires a total order, learner authorization, and a defined view of concurrent additions. The cursor does not govern progress-write idempotency.

options.text: Order by completion time plus module ID and encode both in the cursor to break ties.
Order pages only by completedAt and use that value as the next cursor.
Reuse one global history cursor across learners and rely on each client to filter its own item IDs.
Assume stable cursor paging also makes repeated completion writes idempotent.
Use offset pages over a live list and allow concurrent new completions to shift later pages.

questions.prompt: A learner’s history endpoint lists completed modules. Multiple completions can share the same timestamp, and the learner may add new completions while paging. The endpoint must never show another learner’s records. What query contract makes the history stable and scoped?

feedback.details: Use revision as the primary page boundary and a unique tie-breaker where needed; bind the cursor to the feed filters and snapshot/version. On checkout, validate the authoritative current revision or use a conditional price token before charging. A page can be consistently ordered and still be stale relative to a later publish.

messages.text: Rows may move as prices change, and a feed item is not proof it is still the authoritative checkout price.
Timestamp alone does not define a unique monotonic revision order or prevent a stale price from being accepted.
A cursor identifies read position; it does not prove the price is still current at charge time.
A client may not have received a newer committed revision; only the authority can validate current price.

feedback.reason: The feed needs deterministic immutable revision paging, but checkout freshness is a write/charge precondition. Keep cursor traversal and price authorization distinct.

options.text: Page immutable price revisions by revision ID, not a moving offset into the current price.
Use offset pagination over the mutable current-price table and let checkout trust the price on the page.
Page by publish timestamp alone, which can tie or arrive out of order across publishers.
Treat possession of a valid feed cursor as approval to charge the price returned on that page.
Fetch several pages and let the client choose the highest revision it has seen without validating with the price owner.

questions.prompt: A merchant’s price feed contains immutable revisions. Checkout may process a new revision while a client is still paging through older feed entries. What paging and write contract prevents a stale feed page from authorizing an obsolete price?

feedback.details: Derive account scope from the authenticated principal, cap each page, and use a unique session ID after creation time to avoid ties. Return an as-of/watermark when the index can lag. A session absent from the list may be a projection issue; the authorization owner must check revocation epoch/status on each protected request.

messages.text: Protected session metadata has already crossed the tenant/account boundary before client filtering.
Tied timestamps do not define a deterministic continuation point.
Listing sessions does not make authorization checks reject a token; the security owner must enforce revocation.
This violates the stated 100-row bound and increases the exposure and cost of the read.

feedback.reason: The endpoint is an account-scoped bounded listing. Deterministic paging and watermark expose the list view, while credential revocation remains an enforcement rule at authorization time.

options.text: Bind the cursor to the authenticated account and stable session ordering; reject cross-account reuse.
Search sessions globally and remove other accounts’ rows in the client after receiving the page.
Use createdAt alone as the cursor boundary even though many sessions can share the same timestamp.
Treat the paginated session listing as the mechanism that invalidates a revoked credential.
Return every session for the account in one response and ask the client to find revoked entries.

questions.prompt: An identity service lists sessions for one authenticated account. The list is capped at 100 rows and paged by creation time. Revoked sessions must still be rejected by authorization checks even when the listing index is delayed. Which read contract is appropriate?

feedback.details: Order by immutable createdAt plus unique jobId and define whether pages scan a fixed snapshot or reflect current status. Keep status fields visible without using mutable status as the sort key. The presence of a job in the list does not guarantee a worker lease/recovery path; that must be verified separately.

messages.text: Timestamp ties can skip jobs or cause the same job to recur on later pages.
A row’s position can change during paging, breaking stable continuation.
A list proves only that a record is visible; worker leases and durable job ownership are a separate contract.
Changes can shift offsets, producing duplicates or omissions across the operator’s scan.

feedback.reason: The operator needs deterministic status listing, not a worker lifecycle guarantee. A stable immutable creation key and job ID provide a repeatable cursor; recovery remains another owner contract.

options.text: Order jobs by creation time and job ID, and bind the cursor to the operator’s filter scope.
Use only createdAt as the cursor, so every job with the same timestamp is treated as one boundary.
Order by mutable status and use that status as the continuation cursor while jobs transition from running to done.
Assume that because an acknowledged job appears in a paginated list, its worker will recover after a crash.
Use offsets over a live list and allow new jobs or status changes to shift the result between pages.

questions.prompt: A media service lists transcoding jobs for an operator. Jobs can share a creation timestamp, and the operator needs a stable page boundary while jobs continue to finish. Worker recovery is tracked elsewhere. What list query contract fits?

feedback.details: Bind the query to cohort, policy revision 72, filters, and stable sort; use a snapshot or explicit as-of boundary. New decisions after the boundary belong to a later scan. This yields a reproducible audit page sequence. It does not reverse stored values; compatible persistence and flag rollback require a separate rollout design.

messages.text: Pages can then combine decisions made under different rule revisions, so the audit is not a coherent view.
Paging stabilizes the read only; it cannot make incompatible persisted data reversible.
Concurrent writes can cause duplicates or gaps, and the scan loses its audit revision boundary.
The query is unbounded and client sorting cannot restore a consistent policy snapshot.

feedback.reason: The audit list must represent one cohort/policy view during concurrent writes. Revision pinning and a snapshot boundary keep that query coherent; rollback safety is independent of list pagination.

options.text: Pin the scan to policy revision 72 and page with a deterministic decision ID tie-breaker.
Evaluate each page against the latest policy as it is fetched and display all rows as one cohort audit.
Treat a stable audit cursor as proof that disabling the rollout can reverse any persisted data changes.
Use offset paging without pinning the policy revision, then let new decisions shift the remaining rows.
Download every cohort decision without a row cap or snapshot and let the client sort the export.

questions.prompt: A rollout dashboard lists decisions for one cohort at policy revision 72. New decisions may be written during the scan. The audit must show which rules revision produced each result; the feature itself must remain reversible. What query contract should the dashboard use?

feedback.details: Use startTime plus unique slotId for a complete order and include the projection’s as-of age. Before showing confirmed, perform an atomic reservation that rejects overlaps at the resource owner. Two clients can page the same candidate, so a read or client-side check cannot claim it. The read cursor and the write invariant solve different problems.

messages.text: The 15-second-old projection may already be claimed; listing a candidate is not ownership of the time range.
Ties can lead to missing or repeated candidates across pages.
The caller cannot interpret a potentially 15-second-stale candidate or know when to revalidate.
Other clients have independent views; only the authoritative reservation boundary can serialize conflicting bookings.

feedback.reason: The page is a read candidate set with bounded staleness. Deterministic ordering and freshness help the UI, while atomic reservation at the resource owner enforces no-overlap.

options.text: Use start time plus slot ID as the keyset order and revalidate availability at booking.
Treat a slot’s presence on any page as a reservation and allow the UI to confirm it without a write-side check.
Use startTime alone as the cursor and omit slotId when multiple slots share the same time.
Return a normal available result without saying when the slot projection was produced.
Let each browser check its displayed list for overlaps and submit an unconditional booking if none is visible.

questions.prompt: A booking UI pages through candidate slots for one resource. Results are sorted by start time and may be 15 seconds stale; two users can see the same candidate. What read and write contracts should the API expose?

feedback.details: Include the normalized filters, sort definition, index version/watermark, last unique sort key, and expiration in the cursor. Reject or restart when its index view expires or changes. Return the applied watermark so a caller can distinguish a valid page from a stale projection. Not-found in a lagging index is not proof of source absence.

messages.text: The next page would continue a different query and can skip, repeat, or expose unrelated results.
A watermark without a stable continuation key does not prevent offset shifts or tie ambiguity.
A cursor records continuation context, not completeness; indexing may still lag the source.
An index rebuild can change order and membership; an expired/version-mismatched cursor must not silently continue.

feedback.reason: An opaque cursor is a continuation token for one exact query over one index view. Binding query, ordering, version/watermark, and expiry preserves meaning and makes lag observable.

options.text: Bind the cursor to filters, sort, index watermark, and expiry; reject changed context.
Store only the last sort key and allow the caller to change filters or sort on the next page.
Pin the index watermark but use an offset over rows that can change with indexing and sorting.
Treat a valid cursor as proof that the source and index contain every matching record.
Keep cursors valid forever across index rebuilds and continue against whatever index version is current.

questions.prompt: A search request uses filters F and sort S against an index currently at watermark 812. A cursor may be reused for only 10 minutes. What must the opaque search-after cursor bind so later pages neither change query meaning nor hide indexing lag?

feedback.details: Use priority plus a monotonically assigned arrival sequence as the ordered key, cap the page, and expose queue age for operators. This makes later pages deterministic and preserves urgency ordering. It does not reserve CPU: urgent capacity must be protected by the route compute admission policy rather than inferred from a paginated GET.

messages.text: The ordering ignores the priority distinction the operator needs to see.
Equal priorities lack deterministic continuation and can move unpredictably between pages.
A read page cap does not control the compute admission or worker capacity of those jobs.
An unbounded response increases query cost and transfers server-side queue semantics to each client.

feedback.reason: The listing needs stable priority and sequence ordering with bounded work. It is observational; CPU isolation for urgent routing is enforced independently at admission and execution.

options.text: Order by urgency and arrival sequence, using both values in a stable bounded cursor.
Sort only by arrival time so a long low-priority backlog always precedes newly queued urgent plans.
Sort only by priority and omit a stable sequence for equal-priority plans.
Assume capping the GET /jobs page also limits how much CPU queued route computations can consume.
Return the full route-plan queue and let the client sort it by priority and age.

questions.prompt: A dispatch operator lists queued route plans by urgency. Each plan has a priority and arrival sequence; urgent route computation has its own reserved CPU budget. What query contract keeps job listing deterministic without implying the list protects urgent execution?

feedback.details: Authorize the account and page by immutable creation time plus unique intent ID. A timeout does not mean the charge failed; keep the existing intent UNKNOWN/PENDING and reconcile it using the same provider identity before a new charge. A correct cursor helps find the attempt but is not the idempotency mechanism.

messages.text: Timestamp ties can break paging, and a history page cannot establish that an unknown prior charge failed.
Pagination controls which records are listed; only the effect owner’s stable intent/idempotency contract prevents a second charge.
Amount/time matching is ambiguous and exposes cross-customer metadata; history must be account-scoped.
Concurrent additions can shift page positions, repeating or omitting intents.

feedback.reason: The history is a scoped deterministic read, while duplicate-charge prevention belongs to the stable payment intent and provider reconciliation path.

options.text: Keep UNKNOWN intents in the history and page by creation time plus intent ID.
Page by creation timestamp alone and start a new payment intent whenever the old one is not on the current page.
Assume a correct intent-history cursor deduplicates provider side effects when the customer retries.
Query a provider-wide transaction list and let the client locate its own payment by amount and approximate time.
Use offset pages over a live intent list while new attempts are added, with no deterministic tie-breaker.

questions.prompt: A customer views payment intents ordered by creation time. A provider response timed out for one intent, so its charge outcome is unknown. How should the history query page the intents, and what separate rule protects against a duplicate charge?

feedback.details: Partition by risk priority and order within each band by stable arrival sequence/event ID. Apply a bounded fairness rule so routine cases make progress while high-risk cases retain priority. Query only the durable queue; a page cannot repair an earlier false ACK. This separates admission guarantee from analyst view ordering.

messages.text: Equal risk scores have no deterministic order, so cases can be skipped or repeated.
A long low-risk queue can starve the cases that the workflow prioritizes.
A query cannot retroactively guarantee that an earlier acknowledgment had durable storage.
Strict priority can starve routine work indefinitely, contrary to the fairness requirement.

feedback.reason: The page must reflect risk priority with repeatable ordering and a fairness boundary. It only lists durable accepted cases; durability is established at admission, not by sorting.

options.text: Page high-risk first with a bounded fairness rule that still admits routine cases.
Sort only by risk score and use that possibly repeated value as the cursor.
Use global FIFO so routine backlog always precedes newer high-risk cases.
Treat appearing on an analyst page as proof the original submission was durably accepted.
Always drain high-risk cases first and never service lower-priority cases while any high-risk item exists.

questions.prompt: Fraud analysts page a backlog that includes high-risk and routine cases. High-risk cases must appear first without starving routine work forever, and acknowledged cases must already be durably admitted. What listing contract should the API provide?

feedback.details: Resolve the exportId to snapshot 550 and rules revision 17, and use a stable rowId tie-breaker for paging. Persist page boundaries or use a cursor scoped to that immutable artifact. A retry after the source advances to 557 still reads the original export. A new corrected export receives a new identity rather than silently changing page 2.

messages.text: The retry would splice newer rows into the original artifact and break reproducibility.
Corrections can shift row positions and change which records appear on page 2.
A period does not identify the source snapshot or calculation rules that produced the first page.
Client sorting cannot reconstruct the pinned historical snapshot after rows have changed.

feedback.reason: An export is a reproducible artifact, not a live view of a payroll period. Pinning the snapshot, rules, and cursor keeps all pages on the same accepted result.

options.text: Bind every page to the same export ID, source snapshot, rules revision, and row cursor.
Recompute page 2 from snapshot 557 because it is the latest payroll state for the same period.
Use offset paging over the current payroll table without pinning a snapshot or rules revision.
Bind the cursor to period 2026-09 alone and let the export rules revision default to the current value.
Return an unbounded set of rows and let the client sort and deduplicate after receiving all current versions.

questions.prompt: Payroll rows for period 2026-09 were exported from source snapshot 550 under rules revision 17. A client retries page 2 after a partial download, while later payroll corrections have produced snapshot 557. Which paging contract preserves one export?

feedback.details: Create a report snapshot or cutoff before page 1 and embed its identity plus filters and continuation key in each cursor. Include the as-of watermark in responses. If the snapshot expires, return an explicit restart/expired result or create a new report ID; do not mix current page data into the old report. Separate table cutoffs are not a coherent financial snapshot.

messages.text: Page 2 may include entries absent from page 1, so the combined report no longer represents one cutoff.
A stable row key does not freeze the source state across pages.
Different cutoffs can combine values that never coexisted and break reconciliation.
The same report identity would then refer to mixed or changing output without telling the caller.

feedback.reason: The report total and every page must share one source cutoff. A snapshot-bound cursor gives page continuity and auditability while making freshness explicit.

options.text: Pin all pages to the same accounting cutoff and continue with a deterministic keyset.
Read each page from the latest accounting state when requested and combine them under the original report ID.
Store only the last row key in the cursor and read later pages from whatever snapshot is current.
Page each underlying table from its own newest watermark and sum the resulting aggregates.
If the cursor expires, silently restart page 2 from the latest snapshot but retain the same report ID.

questions.prompt: A financial report returns page 1 from an accounting snapshot at cutoff 2026-09-30T23:59Z. New entries arrive before page 2 is requested. Both pages must reconcile to one report total. What pagination contract should the API use?

feedback.details: Constrain the time window and response cost, and use eventId after eventTimestamp to establish a total order. Return the ingestion watermark or as-of state so callers know which source events are included. Keep query-serving connections separate from bursty ingest admission; LIMIT alone cannot protect a shared pool.

messages.text: Timestamp ties make the boundary ambiguous and can omit or repeat events.
This ignores the stated cost bound and can monopolize query resources.
An ingest burst can consume the query budget despite a bounded result page.
The caller cannot distinguish a complete time range from events not yet indexed.

feedback.reason: A deterministic event key and explicit query budget make time-series reads repeatable and bounded. Capacity isolation and watermark report the ingestion/read relationship.

options.text: Order by event time and event ID; bound the requested time range and cursor lifetime.
Continue pages using eventTimestamp alone even when many measurements have the same timestamp.
Allow any historical time range and return every matching event in one response.
Run reads through the same worker/connection pool used to absorb producer bursts.
Return a bounded page without indicating how far ingestion has applied and imply it includes all current source events.

questions.prompt: Analysts query telemetry by event time. Multiple events share timestamps, and ingestion bursts must not consume the query-serving connection pool. The query has a maximum time range and row budget. What read contract fits?

feedback.details: Authorize the tenant on the server and order by attemptTime plus unique attemptId. Bind the cursor to tenant and filters and cap each page. Separately set provider deadlines, bounded in-flight work, and a provider-specific circuit policy so delivery slowness cannot exhaust request workers. A paginated history does not impose those runtime limits.

messages.text: The read crosses the trust boundary before filtering; tenant scope must be enforced by the server.
Tied timestamps cannot uniquely locate the next page boundary.
Read pagination does not control outbound provider concurrency or request-worker isolation.
The result is unbounded and may reveal unrelated notifications while consuming excessive query capacity.

feedback.reason: The audit list needs tenant-scoped deterministic paging. Slow provider isolation is an independent outbound-call contract, not a property of the read cursor.

options.text: Page attempts by delivery ID and attempt sequence within the authorized tenant.
Query attempts across tenants and ask the administrator’s browser to remove rows outside its tenant.
Use attemptTime alone as the cursor even when multiple attempts share the same timestamp.
Assume that paging the attempt log limits how many provider calls can be in flight.
Return every attempt for every notification in a single response and let the client sort locally.

questions.prompt: An administrator pages delivery attempts for one tenant and needs deterministic history. A slow notification provider must not block request workers. What query contract should the attempt list use, and which issue remains separate?

feedback.details: Use sequence as the total order and pin the page set at 9200, with a bounded page size and cursor bound to tenant/filter context. Enforce authorization before returning records and apply the retention policy consistently. New events belong to a later scan. The read contract cannot repair a record that was never durably appended or restore a deleted/tampered record.

messages.text: Wall-clock time may not define a unique total order or match the ledger’s authoritative append sequence.
Other tenants’ audit records have already been disclosed before client-side filtering.
The reviewer asked for an as-of boundary; including later entries changes the reviewed set mid-scan.
An immutable ledger still follows its declared retention and access obligations; immutability is not unlimited retention.

feedback.reason: Monotonic sequence and an as-of boundary produce a stable ledger scan. Tenant authorization and retention remain server-side policy constraints.

options.text: Capture a ledger sequence cutoff and page entries by tenant plus sequence.
Order by event wall-clock timestamp and use it as the only cursor despite clock skew and tied times.
Read a global page and let the reviewer filter out entries belonging to other tenants.
Use sequence 9200 as a starting point but let later appended entries enter later pages of the same review.
Prevent all retention expiry and access-policy enforcement so every ledger row remains visible indefinitely.

questions.prompt: An audit ledger is append-only and retained by policy. A reviewer needs to list entries for one tenant as of ledger sequence 9200, in stable pages, without seeing another tenant’s entries. What query contract is needed?

feedback.details: Use the carrier’s sequence/revision as the business order and eventId as a deterministic tie-breaker. Include arrival metadata separately when operators need it. The authoritative projection writer compares the incoming revision atomically with stored state and ignores/quarantines lower revisions. A stable history cursor helps explain out-of-order delivery but does not prevent regression by itself.

messages.text: A late delivery can arrive after a newer carrier state and move the parcel backward.
Without a stable tie-breaker, page continuation can skip or duplicate same-sequence events.
Read ordering does not control the update transaction; the projection writer must enforce monotonic revision.
Storage order is not a declared business order and the unbounded response is hard to page repeatably.

feedback.reason: The event feed needs a deterministic source order, while the current-state projection needs its own monotonic write guard. Sorting a read page cannot enforce a state transition.

options.text: Show carrier history in carrier revision order while separately exposing the current projection.
Sort by receiver arrival time and overwrite current shipment state with the last event returned.
Use carrier sequence alone even when multiple event types share one sequence value.
Assume that sorting history pages by sequence automatically prevents the write-side projection from regressing.
Return all events in storage order and let clients infer the carrier’s progression.

questions.prompt: A parcel history lists carrier events, which may arrive out of order. The history should show carrier order, while the current shipment projection must never regress. How should paging and projection ordering be defined?

feedback.details: Keep v1 behavior stable for existing readers, and add an explicit v2 cursor contract with query binding and index watermark. Run both during the migration window, observe client usage and correctness, and document the retirement condition. A server-side version adapter may be used, but returning only cursor fields to v1 readers breaks them. Compatibility should be evidence-based, not permanent by default.

messages.text: Old clients still send offset requests and cannot continue pagination after the one-sided cutover.
Adding a response field does not preserve the old request/response behavior if offset stops working.
This avoids an immediate break but leaves permanent ambiguous support and operational cost.
A cursor bound to no index view may continue against different membership/order and hide lag.

feedback.reason: Old v1 clients coexist with the new index, so preserve their observable contract while introducing the cursor version. Retire offset only after measured adoption and a defined support boundary.

options.text: Keep v1 offset behavior; add a versioned cursor contract with watermark and dual support during migration.
Deploy cursor-only responses immediately and require every client to upgrade in the same release.
Add a cursor field to the v1 response and assume old clients will ignore it while the server stops honoring offset.
Keep both contracts indefinitely without tracking adoption or defining a retirement date.
Return a cursor without its index version/watermark and assume clients can continue across index rebuilds.

questions.prompt: Search API v1 accepts offset=100. A new index supports opaque search-after cursors and returns a source/index watermark. Old mobile clients remain active for a month. How should the API evolve without breaking those readers?

feedback.details: Define what missing confidence means, deploy readers that accept the field when present and absent, then allow writers to populate it. Leave duration’s existing meaning untouched. Validate old-reader behavior with the actual v1 contract. Additive syntax alone is not enough when readers reject unknown fields or new readers assume the field always exists.

messages.text: Old clients may reject an unknown required field, so the rollout depends on a coordinated upgrade that is unavailable.
Old readers still interpret duration as time, so changing its meaning corrupts their result.
Old payloads omit the value during coexistence, so the new reader fails its own compatibility window.
Indefinite duplicate fields create conflicting sources of truth instead of a staged optional migration.

feedback.reason: Both reader behaviors are explicit: old clients ignore unknown optional fields and new clients tolerate absence. An additive optional field with a documented default preserves both directions of coexistence.

options.text: Add optional etaConfidence with a documented default; keep old response fields and readers valid.
Make etaConfidence required and deploy writers that always send it before old readers are upgraded.
Reuse duration as the confidence value and document the changed interpretation for new clients.
Deploy new readers that require etaConfidence before any writer sends the optional field.
Add etaConfidenceV2 and keep multiple confidence fields forever without deciding which is authoritative.

questions.prompt: Route planning response v1 contains routeId and duration. V2 adds optional etaConfidence; old readers ignore unknown optional fields and new readers default the field when absent. No coordinated deployment is possible. What migration is safest?

feedback.details: Persist paymentIntentId and the provider request before calling the provider. For an unknown response, return the specified nonterminal 503 plus status Location and hold the original intent; do not report false or create a second charge until reconciliation establishes the result. V2 may represent PENDING/UNKNOWN directly. A retry must query or resume the same stable intent, not create a new one.

messages.text: Encoding unknown as false triggers the legacy reader’s retry path; it may create another charge for the unresolved paymentIntentId.
Unversioned values do not solve v1’s false-as-final behavior; retain the v1 status-location path and expose new states through the staged v2 contract.
A timeout is ambiguous, not proof of no charge; false would collapse unknown into failure.
A client-side cache cannot establish provider state and leaves the server contract unable to express uncertainty.

feedback.reason: A boolean false is terminal to the old reader, while a timeout does not prove the provider declined the charge. A nonterminal 503 with a status Location lets v1 resolve the same paymentIntentId without launching another charge.

options.text: Keep one paymentIntentId and return nonterminal 503 plus status Location until reconciliation; never start a fresh charge.
Encode PENDING and UNKNOWN as false in v1 and let the client decide whether to retry.
Add new enum values to the existing v1 response and assume every old client tolerates unknown values.
Set status=false whenever the provider response times out, even if authorization may have completed.
Keep only the boolean forever and handle pending outcomes in an unrelated client cache.

questions.prompt: Payment API v1 returns a boolean and requires a stable paymentIntentId that can be queried at a status location. A provider timeout can leave the charge outcome unknown; v2 needs PENDING and UNKNOWN. V1 readers treat false as final failure and submit another charge. What compatibility behavior can prevent a duplicate charge?

feedback.details: Version the envelope or add an optional priority with a documented rule for absence. The consumer must safely route or quarantine legacy cases rather than silently demoting them. Upgrade producers, measure which versions still omit the field, and remove the fallback only after coverage is proven. A required field is only safe after old producers are retired.

messages.text: A v1 producer may be sending a high-risk case; the default silently violates its required handling.
Legacy producers remain active, so an immediate hard cutover loses cases during coexistence.
Heuristic parsing can misclassify a high-risk case and gives no consistent migration contract.
Compatibility parsing alone does not preserve the priority behavior the new field was introduced to express.

feedback.reason: Absent v1 priority is ambiguous and cannot safely mean low. Establish an explicit conservative fallback, deploy tolerant readers, then migrate producers with evidence before retiring v1.

options.text: Define a safe absent-priority rule and upgrade readers before producers; quarantine ambiguous high-risk legacy cases.
Default an absent priority to low so legacy messages enter the ordinary queue without delaying.
Reject every v1 envelope as soon as the new consumer launches, without a producer transition window.
Infer priority from arbitrary payload text with no stable schema or audited mapping.
Accept both schemas but route all cases through one FIFO queue regardless of the new field.

questions.prompt: Fraud envelope v1 has caseId and payload. V2 adds priority, but some v1 producers omit it and may send high-risk cases during rollout. The queue must not silently route them as low priority. What compatibility rule should govern migration?

feedback.details: Retain each v1 artifact with its snapshot, rules revision, and schema version. New v2 exports receive an explicit version and new identity; any conversion must state how decimal dollars map to integer minor units and how rows regroup. A retry of an old export returns its original artifact. Updating the serializer in place breaks audit reproducibility.

messages.text: Old readers would misread units, and the archived v1 artifact would no longer preserve its original meaning.
A retry would return different bytes under the same historical identity.
The same request identity would have ambiguous schema and amount units.
Without provenance, auditors cannot reproduce or interpret the original v1 output.

feedback.reason: Historical downloads are immutable artifacts with established units and grouping. Version the new representation and keep old export IDs bound to their original bytes and provenance.

options.text: Keep v1 exports immutable and version v2 amount units and row shape under a new export contract.
Change the meaning of amount in place and let existing v1 readers interpret the new integer as dollars.
Recalculate any old export ID using the current v2 grouping and amount representation.
Return either v1 or v2 rows from the same endpoint based on whichever backend is available.
Rewrite historical exports to v2 and discard the original rules/snapshot metadata.

questions.prompt: Payroll export v1 stores amount as decimal dollars. V2 stores integer minor units and changes row grouping. A user may download an old v1 export years later by its export ID. How should the migration preserve audit meaning?

feedback.details: Expose integer minor units with an explicit currency code in a versioned field or endpoint. During coexistence, keep the existing decimal field’s semantics unchanged and document any conversion rounding. Track reader adoption before removing v1. Renaming or changing the unit without a version makes syntactically valid values economically wrong.

messages.text: Old readers will parse cents as whole currency units and misreport the amount.
Old clients can reject the new required shape or still depend on the old field.
Currency is part of the value’s meaning and cannot be safely inferred from presentation settings.
Readers can disagree about which value to trust, leaving a permanent contract ambiguity.

feedback.reason: A numeric value is not interpretable without its unit and currency. Version the changed representation and preserve v1 semantics until old readers are safely retired.

options.text: Add a versioned amount representation with explicit currency and minor-unit meaning.
Change the existing total field from decimal units to integer cents without changing its name or version.
Add a required cents field to the current response and stop returning the old decimal field immediately.
Send the integer total but infer currency from locale or a client preference.
Return both decimal and minor-unit fields indefinitely without specifying which is canonical.

questions.prompt: A financial API v1 returns totals as decimal currency units. V2 needs integer minor units and explicit currency; some readers still parse the v1 decimal field. How should the schema evolve?

feedback.details: Specify the semantics when deviceMetadata is absent, then test v1 producer→new consumer and v2 producer→old consumer with real serializers. Add the field without changing existing event meaning. Backfill only when the source contains authoritative metadata; otherwise retain absence. A staged producer rollout can begin after readers tolerate both forms.

messages.text: Old producers remain active, so the new consumer would reject valid messages during coexistence.
The assumption is unverified; old consumer behavior is a compatibility fact to test, not infer from additive syntax.
Guessed backfill invents source facts and can corrupt analytics.
The rollout still includes v1 producers, so a required field breaks legitimate old writes.

feedback.reason: Optional metadata is compatible only if absence and unknown-field behavior are defined at both reader generations. Test the old/new directions and avoid inventing values for historical events.

options.text: Make deviceMetadata optional with defined absence semantics for old producers and consumers.
Deploy new consumers that reject v1 events without deviceMetadata.
Send the field to old consumers without checking whether their deserializers reject unknown properties.
Populate missing historical metadata with a guessed device value so every old event appears complete.
Make deviceMetadata required for all producers before old producers have a migration path.

questions.prompt: Telemetry event v1 has deviceId and eventTime. V2 adds optional deviceMetadata. Old producers remain active, and new consumers must accept v1 events; during rollout, old consumers may receive v2 events. What compatibility tests and field rule are needed?

feedback.details: Keep one deliveryId for the notification across retries. New readers can use RETRY_PENDING; old readers need a documented nonterminal response and status location so they can query the same delivery rather than resubmit it as new. Do not claim delivered before provider acceptance or convert an in-progress delivery to terminal failure. If an old request cannot be matched to a stable deliveryId, fail closed without creating another provider delivery; do not guess that the old request is new.

messages.text: Old clients interpret false as final failure and may create a second notification while the original is retrying.
The described readers do not have that behavior; unversioned expansion may trigger unsafe retry logic.
That falsely claims the provider delivered the notification before confirmation.
Local state cannot reconcile the sender and provider. If a legacy request cannot be matched to a stable deliveryId, fail closed rather than create another delivery.

feedback.reason: Mapping pending to false triggers old callers to create another delivery; mapping it to true falsely claims provider success. A stable delivery identity and a nonterminal resolution path avoid both errors.

options.text: Expose RETRY_PENDING through a staged contract and resolve old-client retries against the same delivery ID.
Map RETRY_PENDING to delivered=false in v1 and let old clients submit a new delivery.
Add RETRY_PENDING to v1 and assume old clients will handle the unknown status safely.
Map RETRY_PENDING to delivered=true so old clients do not retry.
Keep the server boolean unchanged and store pending state only in the current client’s local cache.

questions.prompt: Notification delivery v1 has a stable deliveryId and status location. V2 must expose RETRY_PENDING without claiming provider success. Old clients treat false as terminal failure and immediately resend. How should the migration prevent duplicate delivery?

feedback.details: Introduce a versioned event contract with server-bound principal identity for new appends. Keep readers able to interpret legacy events with an explicit unknown actor state. Migrate historical rows only when trusted audit evidence maps them to a principal; never fill gaps with a guessed service account. Retire old writers after observed adoption and a documented transition.

messages.text: A default would fabricate attribution for actions whose actor is unknown.
Old producers/readers coexist and a hard cutover can lose valid in-flight audit history.
Presence is not provenance; the authenticated principal must be bound to the event.
This does not establish the new attribution requirement or provide a retirement condition.

feedback.reason: The actor field is evidence, not decoration. Require authenticated attribution for new events and preserve honest unknown status for legacy records unless authoritative evidence supports migration.

options.text: Require authenticated actor IDs for new writes; reject ambiguous legacy events without fabricating history.
Rewrite every historical missing actor as “system” so the new mandatory field is populated.
Reject every legacy event and reader immediately because new records require an actor ID.
Make actorId mandatory in the payload but trust whatever identifier an unauthenticated client supplies.
Keep actor optional for all new events and never measure whether old producers have migrated.

questions.prompt: An audit event is changing from optional actor metadata to a mandatory authenticated actor identifier. Historical records may lack that identity, and the source cannot prove who performed some actions. What schema migration is defensible?

feedback.details: Keep the current shipment state unchanged for any revisionless event during migration. Upgrade producers to include stable event IDs and an authoritative monotonic shipmentRevision, verify all active writers provide it, then make receiver validation mandatory. A quarantined event can be replayed only after its source order is established; deduplication handles repeated identity but does not establish order.

messages.text: This rejects legacy traffic without first preserving it in a quarantine/replay path; it can lose updates during the overlap.
Assigning revision zero is unsafe, and accepting the event can overwrite current state; quarantine it instead.
Arrival time is not source order, so a delayed old update can overwrite the latest shipment state.
Deduplication suppresses a repeated event ID but provides no ordering proof for a distinct revisionless event.

feedback.reason: A revisionless delivery has no ordering evidence, so neither arrival time nor a default value can prove it is newer. Quarantine it until its authoritative revision can be verified.

options.text: Quarantine revisionless carrier events until a verifiable source revision is supplied and coverage is proven.
This rejects legacy traffic without first preserving it in a quarantine/replay path; it can lose updates during the overlap.
Assigning revision zero is unsafe, and accepting the event can overwrite current state; quarantine it instead.
Arrival time is not source order, so a delayed old update can overwrite the latest shipment state.
Deduplication suppresses a repeated event ID but provides no ordering proof for a distinct revisionless event.

questions.prompt: Carrier producers are gradually adding shipmentRevision. Old and new producers may overlap, deliveries can be duplicated or delayed, and revision will become required for monotonic state enforcement. Until every producer sends a verifiable revision, how must the receiver handle a revisionless delivery so it cannot overwrite current shipment state?

feedback.details: For v2, persist operationId and its request parameters before the provider call, return the existing job for an identical retry, and reject reuse with changed parameters. For a legacy timeout or retry whose intent cannot be matched, return/retain UNKNOWN or reject it without another billable side effect; do not guess identity from file content or create a fresh job. Track legacy usage, provide a bounded migration window, and require stable operationId before further billable execution.

messages.text: A new job ID makes an ambiguous retry look like a new intent and can cause a second provider charge.
File equality does not identify the requested operation; deduplicating by content can suppress a legitimate new extraction and still cannot resolve an unknown prior charge.
An immediate global cutoff is not a measured migration; preserve non-billable status access and move callers to stable operation IDs on a bounded schedule.
An unbound or changed operationId cannot identify the original billable intent; persist and compare request parameters before replay.

feedback.reason: Without stable identity, the service cannot tell a retry from a new extraction. Calling the billable provider again could charge twice, so the ambiguous attempt must remain unresolved until the same intent is identified.

options.text: Hold unmatched legacy retries UNKNOWN without a provider call; require a stable operationId before billable execution.
A new job ID makes an ambiguous retry look like a new intent and can cause a second provider charge.
File equality does not identify the requested operation; deduplicating by content can suppress a legitimate new extraction and still cannot resolve an unknown prior charge.
An immediate global cutoff is not a measured migration; preserve non-billable status access and move callers to stable operation IDs on a bounded schedule.

questions.prompt: An extraction API v1 may retry by creating a new job ID, and some active legacy callers provide no stable intent identity. feedback.details: Persist the allocation intent before contacting the inventory authority. If an old request cannot be matched to its stable allocation intent, fail closed and hold it for reconciliation; do not allocate a new seat under a guessed identity.
