Queue acceptance is not a completed reservation and can produce a false ticket confirmation.
Old clients may reject new values or treat them as failure and trigger duplicate allocation.
Client-local state cannot query the inventory authority. If the request cannot be matched to its stable allocation ID, hold/fail closed instead of creating a second allocation.

options.text: Keep an unknown allocation under one stable intent and status location; never map it to terminal failure.
Map every timeout to failed in v1 and ask the old client to retry with a new request.
Return allocated as soon as the request is accepted into a queue, before the seat claim commits.
Add pending and unknown to the v1 enum without testing old client behavior.
Keep only the two-state server response and store pending locally on whichever client submitted the request.

feedback.details: Derive tenant authorization from the authenticated identity on the server and check it before querying. messages.text: A permissive default can resolve another tenant’s cases and violates server-side ownership.
An untrusted request field does not establish authorization for that tenant.
Unauthorized records have already been read and may reach logs or caches before filtering.
This may break active clients; safe migration should preserve service only when tenant scope can be proven.

feedback.reason: Tenant scope is a security boundary. Versioning can stage client compatibility, but a legacy request without provable scope must fail closed rather than receive a permissive default.

options.text: Derive tenant scope from authenticated identity and version-gate clients that omit it.
Map a missing tenant to a shared default scope so v1 requests continue to return results.
Accept a tenantId supplied by the legacy client without checking it against authenticated identity.
Run the global search for v1 and filter returned cases by tenant after the query.
Remove v1 immediately without staging clients or a version/access transition.

Treating stale projection as confirmed absence misleads clients and changes the meaning of the existing 404.

How should the contract evolve without changing the established 404/503 behavior?

feedback.details: Upgrade gateways to understand both contracts, then deploy firmware that persists command identity/sequence and rejects already-applied commands. Route replay-sensitive commands only when the target device’s capability is known; otherwise use a safe legacy policy or reject/defer. Measure firmware coverage before making v2 mandatory. A gateway-only dedup table cannot resolve a device crash after actuation but before its response.

messages.text: The old device may reject the message or execute duplicates because it lacks the new replay guard.
The physical effect boundary must also know whether it already acted; gateway delivery records cannot prove device execution.
A constant sequence cannot distinguish a new command from a replay.
The migration lacks evidence that all devices can accept v2 and may interrupt valid control operations.

feedback.reason: The replay guarantee is enforced at the physical effect boundary, and old firmware lacks that capability. Stage rollout by verified device capability instead of assuming the gateway or wire format is enough.

options.text: Stage gateway and device support for command sequence IDs; block unsafe execution on legacy firmware.
Start emitting sequence fields to every device immediately and assume old firmware will ignore unknown fields safely.
Deduplicate at the gateway and declare unsafe replay solved even though the device may execute twice after reconnect.
Assign sequence zero to old firmware commands and let that value authorize repeated actions.
Disable every v1 device immediately without a staged coverage check or fallback.

questions.prompt: IoT command v2 adds command sequence and idempotency identity so devices can reject replay. Gateway readers update before firmware; many devices remain on v1 during rollout. Unsafe repeated actuation must be prevented. What transition policy is required?

feedback.details: Negotiate receiver capability or use an explicit v2 envelope while preserving v1 bytes for old endpoints. Keep one deliveryId across retries and vary attempt metadata separately. messages.text: The prompt says some receivers reject unknown fields, so immediate expansion breaks them.
Attempts for one logical event need the same identity; fresh IDs bypass deduplication.
A parsed ID alone does not prevent duplicate processing unless the receiver enforces it durably.
Permanent untracked variants leave senders unable to know which duplicate-safety contract a receiver supports.

options.text: Add deliveryId and attempt metadata through a compatible payload version; deduplicate by stable identity.
Add deliveryId and attempt to every payload immediately and assume all v1 receivers ignore unknown properties.

Send the v2 field but do not verify that the receiver persists it before its side effect.
Keep two subtly different payloads indefinitely with no receiver capability registry or retirement rule.

questions.prompt: Webhook payload v1 has event type and body. V2 adds stable deliveryId and attempt metadata for receiver deduplication. Some receivers reject unknown fields, so payload compatibility must be staged. What migration is safe?

feedback.details: Set an outbound deadline shorter than 700 ms and make one layer own a maximum of three attempts with jittered backoff for transient failures only. Bound in-flight requests for this provider and report terminal/deferred outcomes. Do not retry validation/auth failures, and do not couple other providers to its breaker. This contains both waiting and retry amplification.

messages.text: Independent retry loops multiply attempts and can exceed both the caller SLA and provider capacity.
The provider is slower than the 700 ms budget, so an unbounded wait consumes shared request capacity.
Permanent errors will not recover through retry and waste the bounded provider capacity.
A provider-specific failure would block unrelated healthy dependencies.

feedback.reason: The provider exceeds the request SLA, so the contract needs a bounded call deadline, one attempt owner, and local isolation. Jitter spreads eligible retries without multiplying them across layers.

options.text: Use one retry owner with a bounded attempt budget and provider deadline; release the caller slot at its SLA.
Let the SDK, gateway, and delivery worker each retry three times whenever the provider misses its deadline.
Wait indefinitely for the provider and hold the gateway request worker until it returns.
Retry timeouts, validation errors, and authentication failures identically until an attempt succeeds.
Use one shared circuit breaker for all providers so repeated timeouts here stop calls to healthy providers.

questions.prompt: A notification provider has a 700 ms caller SLA and usually responds in 1.5 seconds. Only one layer may retry, with at most three attempts and jittered backoff; other providers must keep serving requests. What timeout/retry contract fits?

feedback.details: Persist the operation ID with the immutable payload and authenticated principal in the ledger’s idempotency boundary. A retry with matching parameters returns the original result; a changed actor or event body under A17 is a conflict. The caller may stop waiting, but timeout is not a command to undo the commit. Dedup state must survive process replacement.

messages.text: A new ID describes a second append and can duplicate the same administrator action.
The database already committed the event; a network timeout does not roll back that durable write.
The same operation identity must not let a retry change or forge the actor attribution.
A process restart erases the dedup record even though the durable ledger entry remains.

feedback.reason: The write may already be committed when its response is lost. A stable identity bound to actor and payload makes the retry return that same append rather than duplicate or alter attribution.

options.text: Retry the append with the same operation ID and return the already committed event on replay.
Retry using a fresh event ID so the ledger can distinguish the second request from the first.
Treat the lost response as proof the append did not commit and delete any record matching A17 before retrying.
Reuse A17 but accept the actor name from the retry payload without checking it against authentication.
Remember A17 only in the API process memory and append again after that process restarts.

questions.prompt: An administrator appends an audit event using operation ID A17. The database commits it, but the response is lost; the client retries the same action. The record must appear once and retain actor attribution. What retry contract is required?

feedback.details: Retry only eligible transient failures with the original event ID and source revision. At the shipment owner, compare the incoming revision in the same transaction as the state write. A duplicate ID is a no-op; a lower revision is rejected/quarantined; a higher revision advances state. Never convert a stale conflict into an unconditional retry.

messages.text: A retry becomes indistinguishable from a new update and may bypass dedup or monotonic order.
Delayed revision 41 can arrive after 42 and overwrite newer shipment state.
A stale revision conflict is not transient; removing the precondition causes state regression.
The receiver may not have accepted a transiently delayed event; same-ID retries are safe when receiver dedup and revision checks exist.

feedback.reason: Retry identity handles delivery ambiguity; the revision guard handles ordering between different updates. Preserve both through retry so a late 41 cannot overwrite 42.

options.text: Retry the same event identity and apply only revisions newer than the shipment’s current revision.
Assign a new event ID and reset the revision whenever a delivery times out.
Apply whichever authenticated carrier message arrives last, regardless of its revision.
Retry a conditional-write conflict by dropping the revision precondition and writing the payload.
Drop the update after the first timeout because retries may be duplicated.

questions.prompt: A carrier update with shipment revision 42 times out at the receiver and is retried later; a revision 41 event is also delayed in transit. What retry rule keeps the shipment from regressing?

feedback.details: Persist the intent and provider idempotency key before dispatch. On timeout, report pending/unknown and query or reconcile the same provider operation. Retry only transiently eligible calls under one bounded owner and the same identity. Do not create a new job ID until the prior intent is conclusively resolved as not executed or a new user intent is submitted.

messages.text: The first provider job may already be running, so a fresh identity can create a second charge.
The timeout records loss of a response, not proof the provider did no work.
Unbounded retries amplify load and can repeat billable attempts if the provider lacks perfect dedup.
Unknown is actionable only when the system can query and resolve the original intent.

feedback.reason: The provider may have accepted work before the deadline. Durable identity and reconciliation preserve one billable intent while its result is unknown; the retry budget belongs to one owner.

options.text: Reconcile the existing extraction operation after timeout; do not create a second billable job.
Start a new provider job ID whenever the worker deadline expires.
Mark the job failed at the deadline and tell the client to submit a new extraction.
Retry the provider indefinitely at every worker and client timeout with no shared budget.
Return a generic unknown response but keep no durable operation record to reconcile later.

questions.prompt: An extraction worker times out after the billable provider may have started the job. The client may retry, but the provider outcome can remain unknown for several minutes. What deadline/retry contract avoids duplicate billing?

feedback.details: Persist the allocation intent before calling inventory. If the response is lost, retain its stable identity and report pending/unknown. Query the same operation or reconcile with the inventory owner; only a confirmed no-claim result can become final failure. Bound retries and status polling. Do not use a new identity solely because the caller timed out.

messages.text: The first claim may already have committed, so a new ID can reserve a second seat.
A probable outcome is not an authoritative reservation and may falsely confirm an unallocated ticket.
Repeated allocation attempts can compete for or consume multiple seats.
The caller cannot safely tell whether to wait, retry, or contact support when the state is discarded.

feedback.reason: A deadline cannot decide the inventory result. Exposing pending/unknown under the original operation identity lets the service reconcile without turning an uncertain first claim into another allocation.

options.text: Query the same allocation intent after deadline and keep UNKNOWN until the inventory owner resolves it.
Return failed and instruct the client to retry with a new allocation ID.
Return confirmed whenever the inventory call times out because the seat probably committed.
Repeat allocation at every poll until a success response arrives, without checking the original intent state.
Return only a generic server error and discard the request identity so no status can resolve later.

questions.prompt: A ticket reservation deadline expires after the inventory authority may have claimed a seat. The client must not allocate another seat while the result is uncertain. What response and retry policy is correct?

feedback.details: Derive the tenant from authenticated identity and authorize the case before starting the query. Carry the deadline/cancel signal into database operations and stop work when canceled; ignore late results. If the deadline is exceeded, return a timeout/unavailable outcome scoped to that request. Never broaden a query to meet latency or move tenant filtering to the client.

messages.text: Meeting latency cannot justify crossing tenant scope; an unscoped query exposes protected data.
Uncanceled backend work continues consuming capacity after the caller no longer needs it.
Other tenant data is already disclosed and the authorization decision belongs at the server.
A canceled request is not a transient provider failure; an automatic fresh query defeats cancellation and can amplify load.

feedback.reason: Deadline and cancellation control work lifetime, while tenant authorization is a non-negotiable query boundary. Propagate cancellation without changing the scope predicate.

options.text: Propagate cancellation to the tenant-authorized query and stop work at its 300 ms deadline.
If authorization is slow, run the search without the tenant predicate so the 300 ms deadline is met.
Let canceled searches run to completion in the shared worker pool and return results if they eventually finish.
Return a broad result set before the deadline and rely on the client to hide other tenants’ rows.
Treat cancellation as a query failure and immediately start a fresh unbounded search under a new request identity.

questions.prompt: A tenant-scoped support search has a 300 ms deadline and supports cancellation. Cancellation must stop expensive query work, but it must never skip tenant authorization or return another tenant’s results. What deadline/cancellation contract fits?

feedback.details: Use a finite request deadline. Return metadata with its age when within the 20-second policy; return stale/not-yet-indexed if the projection exceeds it, confirmed 404 only when source absence is known, and 503 when the source cannot answer. Retry only transient failures with a bounded attempt policy. Never turn a dependency outage into absence or retry a permanent 404 forever.

messages.text: A confirmed absent asset is not a transient failure, and unlimited retries consume capacity without changing the result.
The caller cannot rely on the stated freshness bound if stale age is hidden.
Unavailable source state does not prove the asset is absent.
The read has no completion bound and can occupy resources during a two-minute outage.

feedback.reason: Retry depends on outcome class: temporary dependency errors may retry within budget, while not-found and stale states are semantically distinct. A deadline bounds the read even during source outage.

options.text: Retry only explicitly transient source failures; preserve stale, confirmed missing, and unavailable as distinct outcomes.
Retry every not-found response indefinitely until an asset appears.
Serve any cached value as fresh success even when its age exceeds 20 seconds.
Return 404 whenever the source is unreachable so clients can stop retrying.
Wait indefinitely for the source to recover before returning metadata or an error.

feedback.details: Use one operation identity from acceptance through every delivery and device retry. The device records the identity at the physical effect boundary and returns the prior result for a replay. If actuation may have occurred without a recorded response, report unknown and reconcile rather than issuing a fresh command. Bound delivery attempts and distinguish cancel-wait from an explicit command-cancel operation.

messages.text: The prior command may already have executed; a new identity can repeat the unsafe effect.
The cancellation only ends the caller’s wait; delivery or actuation may already have occurred.
The gateway may not know whether the device acted before a response was lost; dedup belongs at the effect boundary too.
Repeated delivery can actuate multiple times, while unbounded attempts overload an offline device path.

options.text: Cancel the caller’s wait without canceling a possibly delivered command; retry with the same device sequence ID.

Treat client cancellation as proof that the device never received or executed the command.
Deduplicate sends at the gateway and assume the device cannot execute a repeated delivery.
Redeliver continuously until the device responds, without a stable identity or bounded retry budget.

feedback.details: Persist the event and delivery state at the sender, retry the same event ID with exponential backoff under one owner, and stop at a declared attempt/time budget with observable dead-letter state. The receiver records the ID and effect intent durably before returning acknowledgment. A timeout remains ambiguous, so a retry is the same event, not a new one.

messages.text: A new ID defeats deduplication and makes retries appear as separate logical events.
Two retry owners can multiply deliveries and overwhelm a recovering receiver.
No backoff or terminal limit creates unbounded load during an outage.
A crash after acknowledgment can lose the event while the sender believes delivery completed.

feedback.reason: At-least-once delivery requires stable identity and receiver dedup. One bounded retry owner with backoff avoids retry amplification while keeping accepted events recoverable.

options.text: Let one sender own bounded retries and let the receiver deduplicate the stable delivery ID.
Generate a fresh event ID on each timeout so every attempt is distinguishable at the receiver.
Let both the sender and receiver retry each other without coordinating attempt counts.
Retry immediately and forever until an HTTP success is observed.
Have the receiver acknowledge after parsing, before its dedup record or side effect is durable.

questions.prompt: A webhook sender receives no acknowledgment before its deadline. Delivery is at-least-once; the receiver deduplicates by event ID. Only one component may own retries, with exponential backoff and a maximum attempt window. What policy should be used?

feedback.details: A retry keeps the same expected revision and operation identity. Retry only transient transport/service failures within the two-attempt budget and one owner. A 412/conflict is not retried as an unconditional write; the client reloads or merges and submits a new intentional edit against the new revision. This prevents late retries from overwriting another collaborator.

messages.text: Removing the precondition converts a detected stale edit into a silent lost update.
Conflicts require a user merge decision; endless attempts cannot make stale content current.
A guessed revision may still be stale and can misrepresent the user’s intended base.
Layered budgets can exceed the intended two attempts and amplify write contention.

After a conflict, retry without If-Match so the user’s edit eventually overwrites the current document.
Retry conflicts, timeouts, and validation errors indefinitely until the write succeeds.
Guess the latest revision from a cache and resend the edit using that value without re-reading the document.
Let both the editor and gateway each perform two retries independently.

questions.prompt: Two collaborators edit revision 28. A stale write returns a version conflict; a network timeout may be transient. The client may retry at most twice, and must never turn a stale edit into an unconditional overwrite. What retry contract fits?

feedback.details: Persist each intent ID so a retry resolves the same reservation, then atomically decrement/claim stock at the inventory owner. Only one transaction can consume the last unit; the other receives conflict or unavailable. Idempotency and deadlines address per-intent repetition and waiting, not cross-intent concurrency.

messages.text: The keys prevent duplicate execution of each intent, not competition between two distinct intents.
A new key may repeat a claim and creates an additional operation instead of resolving the original.
Both distinct requests can read one unit before either transaction commits.
A time budget limits waiting; it does not make the stock mutation atomic.

feedback.reason: Stable IDs make each request retry-safe, but the shared stock invariant spans distinct buyer intents. The authoritative atomic claim is still required.

options.text: Retry each stable reserve intent, but enforce stock availability atomically across distinct buyers.
Assume per-request idempotency keys alone prevent two different buyers from claiming the last unit.
Assign a new key on timeout and retry until each buyer gets a success response.
Read the remaining count before each retry and reserve if it is positive.
Use a short retry deadline as the concurrency control and accept both results if they return before expiration.

questions.prompt: One unit remains in stock. Two distinct reserve intents time out and retry safely by their own IDs. The system must not sell two units or confirm both requests. Which retry boundary is needed?

feedback.details: Persist the submission ID and learner/module binding with the completion result. Do not increment on each attempt or allow another layer to create extra retries. A lost response is not evidence that no completion was stored.

messages.text: The progress counter changes before the response, so ignoring a duplicate response does not undo duplicate increments.
Multiple owners can create more than two attempts and duplicate completion state.
Each identity appears to be a new completion and defeats deduplication of the original intent.
Without durable state, the service cannot know whether to repeat or report the prior result.

feedback.reason: The same learner intent can be delivered more than once. Stable identity and set-state semantics make retries converge, while one bounded owner prevents attempt multiplication.

options.text: Let one service own at most two retries of the idempotent completion set operation.
Send incrementCompletion on every attempt and let the client ignore duplicate response messages.
Let the SDK and progress service each retry twice with independent identities.
Use a new submission ID on retry so each attempt can be audited independently.
Retry a timeout but keep no record of whether the original completion committed.

questions.prompt: A learner submission marks a module complete. The response can be lost, and only the progress service may retry, at most twice. Repeating the same completion must not add progress twice. What retry rule should apply?

feedback.details: Bind the operation identity and revision to the publish request. The price authority applies a conditional monotonic update, and checkout validates the committed revision. Retry transient storage failures at most twice with the same identity. If current revision is already 52, reject stale 51 and report conflict. Cache invalidation can follow but is not publication success.

messages.text: A stale revision conflict is permanent for that payload; unconditional retry would roll the price back from 52.
Independent retry owners exceed the budget and can reorder updates.
The write may have committed before the response was lost; a fresh identity can reapply stale data.
Checkout may still observe the previous revision despite the success response.

feedback.reason: The retry policy must preserve revision order. Retry only eligible transient failures under one bounded owner; a stale revision is a conflict, never an unconditional retry.

options.text: Retry transient publish failures under the same revision precondition; never turn a stale revision into an unconditional write.
On any failure, retry revision 51 as an unconditional overwrite so it can eventually publish.
Let the merchant client and gateway each retry twice with separate revision identities.
Treat a timeout for revision 51 as proof it did not commit, then publish it under a new key.

feedback.details: Use a stable revocation operation and track the epoch/status observed by each relevant enforcement path. Query or retry that same operation; do not allow old sessions because the response was lost. Success means enforcement, not merely queue acceptance.

messages.text: The timeout does not prove enforcement; old sessions may remain authorized after a false success.
A revocation may have committed even though its response was lost, and fail-open behavior preserves risk.
Multiple identities complicate ordering and still do not prove all authorization nodes enforce the revocation.
Unobserved propagation cannot support a success claim or a fail-closed authorization decision.

Return success when the gateway times out so callers stop retrying and assume the old sessions are invalid.
Treat the timeout as proof nothing changed and continue allowing old sessions until a new request arrives.
Create a new revocation operation each time the caller times out and allow nodes to process them independently.
Queue invalidation and provide no status or enforcement watermark, while continuing to accept sessions during lag.

feedback.details: Persist job J8 and its input identity before acceptance. An explicit job-cancel command can change work state separately, with its own race and result semantics.

messages.text: The caller canceled waiting, not the already accepted transcoding operation.
Unbounded recovery can consume resources indefinitely and gives no observable final outcome.
Polling does not create a new intent; another ID can duplicate the same expensive work.
A request deadline measures waiting time and says nothing about job completion.

feedback.reason: The worker job lifecycle is longer than the client wait. Keep accepted state durable, recover workers under a finite policy, and decouple canceling a poll from canceling the job.

options.text: Cancel status polling independently; the durably accepted worker job continues under its own retry policy.
Propagate cancellation of the status poll directly to the worker and delete job J8.
Retry failed transcoding forever with no lease, attempt budget, or terminal status.
Create a new job ID whenever a status poll times out or is canceled.

feedback.details: Set a 100 ms deadline for rule evaluation and return an explicit unavailable outcome if it cannot complete. Keep persisted records readable by old clients independently of the flag. Track rollback as a durable state transition with an observable completion result. Retry an idempotent read within budget if allowed; reconcile an unknown migration outcome before any further write.

messages.text: An ambiguous timeout can repeat an irreversible or non-idempotent migration and break rollback.
Changing the flag does not restore incompatible persisted records.
The required read budget is violated, and waiting does not provide a safe outcome.
Operators and callers cannot tell if the rollout is still active or safely rolled back.

feedback.reason: A rule read may time out, but timeout does not authorize repeating a schema mutation or claiming rollback. Bounded reads and explicit rollback state preserve safety.

options.text: Return an explicit rollback result within deadline and keep persisted data readable by both versions.
Retry the schema mutation after every timeout until it reports success, without checking whether the first attempt committed.

Wait beyond the 100 ms deadline until the rule service responds and keep the request open.
Return a generic error on timeout without recording whether rollback is pending or completed.

questions.prompt: A rollout rule read has a 100 ms deadline. Disabling the feature must produce an explicit rollback result, while persisted records remain readable by old clients. A timeout must not blindly repeat an irreversible schema migration. What retry contract fits?

feedback.details: Keep the same operation ID through each caller retry and resolve it to the recorded attempt. A timeout does not cancel or fail the reservation. At the resource owner, commit only if no conflicting interval exists in the same atomic transaction. Return conflict to the losing intent and confirm only after commit. The retry budget controls attempts, not the invariant.

messages.text: The keys identify different intents and do not enforce the shared resource’s no-overlap invariant.
A retry becomes another reservation attempt and can duplicate or obscure the original result.
The original write may have committed before its response was lost; timeout is an unknown outcome.
Concurrent requests can pass separate reads; only the atomic final write protects the invariant.

feedback.reason: Retries need stable identity, while the overlap rule spans distinct intents. A timeout remains pending/unknown until reconciled; atomic reservation guards each commit.

options.text: Resolve timeout through the same booking intent and atomic overlap guard; do not confirm an unknown result.
Assume distinct idempotency keys make overlapping requests safe and confirm both when their retries succeed.
Generate a new booking ID for each retry so the service can attempt the slot again.
Treat a caller timeout as proof the original reservation did not commit, then release the slot and accept another booking.
Read availability before every retry and confirm if the range looks free.

questions.prompt: Two booking requests for overlapping ranges on the same resource have distinct idempotency keys. One response times out, and each caller may retry twice. What deadline/retry contract preserves no-overlap and avoids duplicate confirmation?

feedback.details: Check per-device budget and command priority before admission. Keep the queue bounded, reserve capacity for urgent commands, and return a visible defer/reject outcome when capacity is unavailable. Use stable command identity at the device/effect owner so retries do not repeat actuation. Do not return success for an unpersisted command.

messages.text: A noisy device can consume the shared budget and delay urgent commands from other devices.
Late quota checks do not protect the bounded queue from overload.
Admission limits request volume but do not deduplicate repeated actuation intent.
A success response falsely acknowledges work that was not durably accepted.

feedback.reason: Admission controls who can consume finite capacity, while device-side dedup protects the physical effect. A quota pass is not an execution or replay guarantee.

options.text: Apply per-device bounded admission with reserved safety-command capacity and explicit defer/reject results.
Use one global rate limit for all devices and return the same response regardless of command priority.
Enqueue each command first, then check whether the device has exceeded its quota.
Assume that a device within quota cannot replay the same physical command more than once.
Return success to every device and drop commands that arrive after queue capacity is exhausted.

questions.prompt: A device control API receives bursts from many devices. Each device has a quota and urgent safety commands take priority; capacity is finite and the device must know whether to retry later. What admission contract should be enforced?

feedback.details: Store events durably with partner identity. Apply per-partner in-flight and attempt budgets and honor receiver Retry-After with bounded exponential backoff. Schedule fairly across partners, and report terminal/deferred states rather than dropping accepted events silently. A global queue without tenant fairness allows one receiver outage to dominate the system.

messages.text: One partner outage can starve all other deliveries and overwhelm shared capacity.
Ignoring Retry-After increases load on an already overloaded receiver.
Quota at delivery time cannot repair loss between the early acknowledgment and durable enqueue.
Accepted durable events cannot be discarded without an explicit terminal/dead-letter outcome.

feedback.reason: Fair per-partner budgets isolate receiver behavior while preserving accepted events. Retry-After and bounded backoff reduce load; durable acceptance happens before quota-governed delivery.

options.text: Enforce each partner’s attempt budget and Retry-After independently; keep accepted events durably queued.
Use a single shared unlimited retry queue and let the busiest partner consume workers until its backlog drains.
Retry every partner at a fixed immediate interval even when its response requests a later retry.
Return accepted to the producer before the event is durable, then apply partner quotas when workers pick it up.
Silently discard a partner’s oldest events when its quota is reached.

questions.prompt: A webhook sender serves many partners. Each partner can impose its own Retry-After and attempt limit; accepted events must survive outages, and one partner’s backlog must not consume every delivery worker. What quota/fairness contract fits?

feedback.details: Cap concurrent write work per tenant/user and schedule fairly across tenants. Every mutation still carries expectedRevision and performs atomic compare-and-swap at the document owner. If admission is deferred, return an explicit result; do not weaken CAS to increase throughput. A global queue can become a noisy-neighbor bottleneck.

messages.text: Admission does not replace the revision invariant; admitted stale writes can still overwrite one another.
This systematically starves smaller tenants rather than providing tenant fairness.
Late admission cannot bound the write load and may already have caused contention or data loss.
Global serialization can let one tenant’s backlog block all others and still needs CAS for stale edits.

feedback.reason: Quota and fairness govern resource access; conditional write governs document correctness. Keep both controls at their respective boundaries.

options.text: Use per-tenant fair admission with compare-and-swap at the document revision owner.
Apply a global quota and let admitted writes use unconditional updates to reduce transaction overhead.
Give the highest-volume tenant the largest share of all write slots to keep its throughput high.
Commit every write first and calculate tenant quota violations asynchronously.
Put every tenant behind one global serial queue with no per-tenant fairness or bounded wait.

questions.prompt: Collaborative editing has a bursty enterprise tenant and smaller tenants. Writes must remain bounded and fair, but concurrent writes based on the same document revision must still conflict rather than overwrite. What admission policy meets both needs?

feedback.details: Bound the queue and concurrency for a hot SKU and return explicit 429/deferred status when its admission budget is full. For an admitted attempt, conditionally decrement/claim stock at the inventory authority. A stale read or quota token cannot promise availability. Separate per-SKU budgets keep one hot item from exhausting unrelated inventory capacity.

messages.text: Quota controls request volume; it does not establish that a unit remains available.
An unbounded backlog can exhaust capacity and gives no bounded overload behavior.
Several requests can pass the same read and overbook the last unit.
A global limit needlessly couples independent resources and harms unrelated buyers.

feedback.reason: Per-SKU admission bounds contention, but the authoritative stock transaction still owns the no-negative invariant. Only commit can justify confirmation.

options.text: Bound the reserve queue per SKU but decide the last unit with an atomic stock claim.
Confirm a reservation whenever the buyer passes the per-SKU rate quota.
Accept every request into an unbounded per-SKU queue and let workers process it later.
Read stock before admission and let each admitted request decrement based on that stale count.
Reject all inventory requests globally when one SKU is hot, including unrelated SKUs with capacity.

questions.prompt: A popular SKU has one unit left and many requests arrive in a burst. The service can queue a bounded number of reserve attempts per SKU, but it must never oversell. Which admission/write policy is correct?

feedback.details: Track request budget per account, calculate it before mutation, and define whether excess work is rejected or durably deferred. Return 429 with a retry policy when not accepted. Reuse the same submission ID for retries and store completion as idempotent state. Never return success for dropped work or 429 after the update has already committed.

messages.text: A throttled or lost-response retry can count the same completion multiple times.
Success claims an update was accepted even though no durable progress state exists.
One account’s burst can consume the shared limit and block unrelated learners.
The side effect already happened; a retry after 429 can duplicate it.

feedback.reason: The quota belongs to the account and must be checked before side effects. Stable identity preserves convergence while an explicit 429/deferred response communicates admission.

options.text: Apply a per-account budget while treating repeated completion sets as the same idempotent operation.
Ask the client to retry every 429 using a new submission ID and increment progress for each attempt.
Return success while discarding requests that exceed the account budget.
Apply one global 30-per-minute limit across all learners.
Write the progress update, then return 429 if the account has exceeded quota.

questions.prompt: A learner account may submit up to 30 progress updates per minute. The service can return 429 or defer accepted work, but a lost response must not lose a completion or count it twice. What budget contract should apply?

feedback.details: Limit each merchant’s bulk update rate and schedule fairly. Keep the authoritative price revision monotonic and tell callers when propagation is delayed. Checkout validates an acceptable revision/age before charge. A larger global quota or unversioned writes do not prevent one merchant’s bulk job from starving others or a retry from publishing old data.

messages.text: A bulk merchant can consume shared capacity and delay checkout freshness for everyone.
Out-of-order bulk retries can restore an obsolete price.
Checkout cannot distinguish committed visible prices from work still waiting in the queue.
A cache can serve an obsolete revision even when a newer publish has committed.

feedback.reason: Per-merchant budgets and fair scheduling contain bulk load; monotonic versioned publication and an observable lag signal preserve checkout correctness.

options.text: Give each merchant a publish budget while checkout reads the latest committed price revision.
Use one global update quota and let bulk updates consume it before checkout reads can validate prices.
Accept all updates without revision checks to maximize throughput.
Queue excess revisions indefinitely but report them as published without a lag/status signal.
Let checkout trust whichever cached price is most recently loaded, without checking its revision or age.

questions.prompt: A merchant bulk-publishes thousands of price revisions, while checkout requires a recently committed price within two seconds. Bulk work may be delayed, but published revisions must be monotonic. What budget policy protects checkout freshness?

feedback.details: Apply per-user or credential-scoped limits before accepting new work. If rate-limited, return a clear 429/retry policy without claiming the change happened. If the operation already committed before a response is lost, resolve the same identity/status rather than treating 429 as undo. Revocation success remains tied to authorization enforcement, not quota admission.

messages.text: The old credential remains usable after the API claims revocation succeeded.
One abusive account can consume the global budget and block unrelated users’ security actions.
Unbounded sensitive operations invite abuse and overload the security path.
A client may interpret 429 as not applied and create another operation; rate decision must precede mutation or report committed result clearly.

feedback.reason: Rate limiting protects the sensitive path, but its response must preserve state semantics. Never say a revocation succeeded until enforcement is in place.

options.text: Apply per-user security budgets without falsely confirming a throttled revocation or reset.
Return success for a revocation that exceeded quota and apply it later when capacity is available.
Use a single global user-change quota shared across all accounts.
Skip rate checks for password reset and revocation because a 429 might frustrate users.
Perform the revocation, then return 429 because the user crossed the request limit.

questions.prompt: Credential changes include revocations and password resets. A user-specific budget is needed to resist abuse, but a throttled revocation must never leave an old credential authorized while returning success. What rate-limit contract is safe?

feedback.details: Estimate CPU/GPU cost per job, enforce per-tenant fairness and a bounded queue, and reserve workers/admission for interactive previews. Persist job identity before acknowledging acceptance. When capacity is full, defer/reject explicitly. Count-based quotas or priority labels alone do not protect a shared hardware bottleneck.

messages.text: A few heavyweight jobs can consume far more resources than their nominal request count suggests.
Autoscaling may lag or hit hardware limits; unbounded admission can exhaust the preview pool.
Priority cannot reserve capacity after heavy jobs occupy all workers.
A restart can lose accepted work before it has a recoverable job identity.

feedback.reason: Weighted admission accounts for heterogeneous resource cost and protects interactive capacity. Durable acceptance ensures accepted jobs can be recovered after restart.

options.text: Use weighted fair worker admission by estimated cost and reserve capacity for interactive previews.
Charge every job one identical quota unit regardless of its CPU/GPU cost.
Accept all GPU-intensive jobs and rely on autoscaling to protect interactive previews.
Mark previews high priority but admit unlimited transcodes into the same workers.
Acknowledge a transcode before its job record is durable, then assign workers based on current load.

questions.prompt: Transcoding jobs vary greatly in CPU/GPU cost, tenants share workers, and interactive preview capacity must remain available. Accepted jobs must survive restart. What admission policy fits?

feedback.details: Set per-operator limits and cap the number of accounts changed in one cohort step. Record operator, cohort, and rule revision for each decision. Advance only after observing the bounded batch and confirming persisted data remains readable under rollback. A rate limit alone does not constrain blast radius, and a flag alone cannot undo incompatible data.

messages.text: A request quota does not bound the blast radius of each admitted rollout.
A flag does not restore incompatible stored records.
The team cannot explain or reproduce which decision caused a cohort change.
Unbounded queued work and premature success hide both capacity and actual rollout state.

feedback.reason: A request quota limits operator activity, while cohort batch size limits impact. Auditable rule revisions and compatible persistence make rollback meaningful.

options.text: Limit rollout by cohort and rate while recording each policy decision under its owning service.
Rate-limit the operator but allow one admitted change to affect all 10,000 accounts at once.
Assume turning off the feature flag reverses any persisted data format change made during rollout.
Apply cohort decisions without recording the rule revision or operator identity.
Queue unlimited cohort mutations and report each as applied when only queued.

questions.prompt: A rollout operator can target cohorts. A broad rollout may affect 10,000 accounts, and rule decisions must be auditable and reversible without incompatible data writes. What quota/control contract should limit blast radius?

feedback.details: Bound each tenant/resource queue, schedule fairly, and return defer/reject when capacity is reached. When a request reaches commit, atomically enforce no overlap at the reservation owner. Admission and slot ownership are separate stages; only the committed transaction permits confirmation.

messages.text: Scheduling order is not the authoritative conflict check; concurrent or retried commits can still overlap.
Queue admission allocates capacity to process a request, not ownership of the time slot.
The unbounded queue can grow without limit and lacks tenant fairness.
Another admitted request can reserve the slot between check and write.

feedback.reason: Fairness controls queue access; the resource’s atomic write controls slot ownership. Keep both in the design and do not confirm at admission.

options.text: Use fair bounded admission per booking resource and preserve an atomic overlap constraint.
Assume fair queue order guarantees that two overlapping bookings cannot commit.
Confirm a booking as soon as it enters its tenant’s fair queue.
Use one unbounded global queue and let the largest tenant submit most requests.
Check slot availability after quota admission, then commit later without an atomic recheck.

questions.prompt: A booking resource has a bounded reservation queue and several tenants compete for slots. Fair admission is required, but overlapping requests must never both be confirmed. What policy is correct?

feedback.details: Apply bounded update/query budgets per index. Keep source writes authoritative even when indexing is throttled, retain change records for replay, and expose the highest applied watermark plus overload/lag. Search can then report stale/not-yet-indexed instead of deleting or denying the source record. Do not claim the index is current based on queue receipt.

messages.text: Index capacity should not decide whether source-of-truth data is accepted or retained.
This hides overload and mislabels projection lag as source absence.
A hot index can starve unrelated indices despite separate workload budgets.
Queued-but-unapplied events have not advanced the searchable watermark; unbounded backlog also hides capacity risk.

feedback.reason: Per-index quotas bound work, while durable source writes and a measurable watermark preserve correctness and freshness reporting.

options.text: Budget index writes and queries separately; expose source durability and the processed watermark.
Reject or delete authoritative source writes whenever the index update quota is reached.
Throttle index updates silently and return a permanent not-found for records beyond the applied watermark.
Use one global query/write quota across every index and let a hot index consume it.
Persist every source event in an unbounded index queue and report zero lag while it waits.

questions.prompt: A search index has separate per-index write and query budgets. When ingestion is throttled, source writes must remain durable and the API must report index lag rather than source deletion. What quota contract fits?

feedback.details: Reserve workers or CPU budget for urgent requests before batch admission. Charge batch work according to expected compute cost and bound its queue; return deferred/rejected when full. Monitor urgent latency and batch wait time. Priority tags without reserved capacity and FIFO queues without class separation cannot prevent starvation.

messages.text: A long batch backlog can place urgent work behind minutes of computation.
A label cannot recover capacity after the shared pool is saturated.
More batch admission increases contention instead of meeting the urgent deadline.
Repeated urgent retries add load to a saturated system and do not create isolation.

feedback.reason: Urgent dispatch has a hard short deadline; batch recomputation is deferrable and expensive. Separate priority capacity and bounded cost admission protect the urgent SLO.

options.text: Keep a reserved urgent route lane and defer bounded batch work under a separate budget.
Put urgent and batch requests in one FIFO queue and process them in arrival order.
Set urgent priority metadata but allow batch work to fill all execution slots and queue indefinitely.
Raise the batch quota whenever requests are rejected, without measuring CPU cost or protecting urgent slots.
Retry every urgent route after 100 ms until one finishes, while leaving batch admission unchanged.

questions.prompt: Route planning has expensive batch recomputation and urgent dispatch with a 100 ms SLO. Batch work may wait, but it must not occupy every worker. What fairness and quota policy should be used?

feedback.details: Check tenant budget before creating a new payment intent. When limited, return 429 with Retry-After or a deferred result. If a provider attempt is already in flight, keep the same intent and provider key, record unknown/pending, and reconcile before retrying. A throttle response must not invite the client to create a second charge.

messages.text: The existing intent may still be pending or charged; a new identity can duplicate the effect.
The charge may already have occurred before quota rejection.
The policy is tenant-specific; global capacity can starve unrelated tenants.
This amplifies overload and abandons deduplication of the original intent.

feedback.reason: Quota admission should stop excess new work before a charge, while existing ambiguous intents retain their identity and reconciliation path.

options.text: Enforce tenant attempt limits while reusing one stable intent across provider 429/503 responses.
Treat 429 as a failed charge and create a new payment intent when the customer retries.
Call the provider first, then reject with 429 if the tenant has exceeded its local budget.
Apply one global attempt cap without tenant scope, allowing a single tenant to consume the shared limit.
Ignore Retry-After and retry 429/503 immediately using a new provider key.

questions.prompt: A tenant’s payment attempts are capped per minute. Provider responses may time out or return 429/503, and the customer must not be charged twice. What quota response and retry rule should the API use?

feedback.details: Persist high-risk case identity before ACK. Use bounded capacity, reserve admission for high-risk work, and schedule bands with a fairness rule that prevents indefinite routine starvation. When low-value capacity is full, return defer/reject rather than silently dropping accepted work. Keep acceptance durability distinct from later analyst throughput.

messages.text: A routine backlog can block high-risk cases that the policy must protect.
Strict priority can starve the lower band indefinitely instead of providing fairness.
Accepted cases must be durable; later silent shedding makes the acknowledgment false.
Priority cannot recover a case lost when the process restarts.

feedback.reason: Durable acceptance protects high-risk cases, while priority bands and fair service distribute scarce processing across classes. Lower-value overload needs an explicit response.

options.text: Reserve durable admission for high-risk cases; defer routine work with explicit backpressure.
Use one FIFO queue for all cases and allow routine traffic to occupy every admission slot.
Always process high-risk cases first and never service routine cases while any high-risk case exists.
Acknowledge all submissions and discard lower-priority cases later if storage fills.
Place high-risk cases at the front of an in-memory queue and return accepted before persistence.

questions.prompt: Fraud review capacity is limited. High-risk cases must persist after acceptance; routine low-value cases may be deferred or rejected. Analysts need fair priority bands rather than one class starving forever. What overload policy meets this?

feedback.details: Estimate/budget export cost and enforce per-tenant/per-period limits before computation. Schedule fairly across tenants. Persist a durable exportId with the period, source cutoff, and rules revision before acknowledging acceptance. If capacity is unavailable, defer/reject visibly. A retry retrieves the pinned artifact; it does not recalculate latest data.

messages.text: A global quota lacks tenant fairness and lets one tenant monopolize expensive export capacity.
The same exportId would then return different bytes and lose historical reproducibility.
Durability alone does not bound costly demand or make queued work running.
The expensive work has already consumed capacity before admission enforcement.

feedback.reason: Export cost is bounded per tenant and period, while stable identity pins the historical output. Admission precedes expensive compute and acceptance records the snapshot.

options.text: Limit exports per tenant and period; pin every accepted job to one immutable snapshot.
Use a single global export quota so a high-volume tenant can consume all available job slots.
When a tenant retries under load, recalculate the export from the latest payroll snapshot to save stored artifact space.
Accept unlimited exports into a durable queue and report them as running before a worker starts.
Calculate the full export first, then reject the tenant if its CPU budget was exceeded.

questions.prompt: Payroll export jobs consume significant CPU. Each tenant may request only a bounded number per period, and accepted exports must remain reproducible under their exportId. What quota contract fits?

feedback.details: Check tenant cost/concurrency budget before running the query. If accepted, bind all reads to one consistent snapshot and return the cutoff. If capacity is unavailable, reject/defer or return cached data with explicit as-of freshness; never mix partial results from different snapshots. Fairness and consistency both need visible contracts.

messages.text: Different source cutoffs can produce a total that never existed at one point in time.
The required fairness is per tenant; global accounting leaves noisy-neighbor behavior.
The caller cannot determine whether the report meets the consistency/freshness requirement.
Late enforcement cannot protect query resources.

feedback.reason: Tenant budgets control cost, and a single snapshot cutoff preserves report meaning. Overload must be explicit or clearly labeled stale.

options.text: Apply a per-tenant cost budget and a consistent cutoff; reject overload before partial totals.
Read whichever table results are available and combine them under one report total when a query exceeds budget.
Use one global budget and let a large tenant consume all query slots.
Return cached results during overload without indicating their cutoff or age.
Run the expensive report and only afterward decide whether the tenant had enough remaining budget.

questions.prompt: Financial report queries have a cost limit per tenant. The report must use one consistent cutoff, and overload may return reject or an explicitly stale result—but must not silently combine snapshots. Which policy is correct?

feedback.details: Keep one authoritative job record and operation ID. Scale GPU workers independently from interactive request handling, and let leases/recovery consume the durable journal after worker replacement. If the workloads shared failure and scaling needs, a split would add network complexity without benefit; here independent GPU pressure and worker lifecycle make isolation useful.

messages.text: The new boundary has no durable job owner, so accepted work can disappear when the API or worker is replaced.
Co-location alone does not meet the independent capacity and failure requirement.
Two job authorities can start duplicate renditions and disagree about status.
Worker lifecycle is exactly the failure mode the durable job journal must survive.

feedback.reason: The prompt gives independent GPU load and worker failure, which justify isolating compute. Durable job identity must remain under one recoverable owner so the split does not lose accepted work.

options.text: Own GPU transcode jobs separately from interactive metadata reads, with durable job status and isolated capacity.
Move orchestration into a separate worker service but leave accepted job state only in the interactive API process.
Keep one service but route GPU work and interactive traffic through the same exhausted worker pool.
Let the API and transcode service each create authoritative job IDs and independently retry missing jobs.
Move both the durable job journal and its ownership to ephemeral workers that restart after each task.

questions.prompt: Video transcoding runs for 25 minutes and consumes GPU, while interactive metadata and playback requests must remain available during worker replacement. The job has a durable journal and can be processed by independent workers. Where should the service boundary sit?

feedback.details: Keep the rule decision and audit revision with the owner that controls persisted rollout state, or split only behind a versioned contract that preserves old-reader behavior and rollback. Use additive/dual-readable data during the rollback window and delay destructive changes. Service boundaries do not provide a migration or undo guarantee by themselves.

messages.text: The flag may roll back while persisted data remains unreadable to old clients.
Feature state and stored data are separate; the flag does not restore an incompatible schema.
Different decisions and revisions can diverge, leaving no clear owner of the cohort state.
A single boundary does not make an incompatible migration reversible.

feedback.reason: The decisive requirement is a coordinated five-minute rollback across flag behavior and persisted data. Cohesive ownership makes the decision/audit path accountable, while compatibility remains a required data contract.

options.text: Keep flag rules and their audit record with the team that owns rollout behavior and compatibility.
Put flag evaluation in one service and schema mutation in another with no coordinated version or rollback contract.
Keep the split but assume setting the flag off automatically reverses the persistence change.
Let both services independently evaluate the rollout rule and write audit records.
Keep one service but perform an irreversible data rewrite before verifying old-reader compatibility.

questions.prompt: A feature rollout rule service and its audit record are maintained by one team. The new flag changes persisted records; turning the flag off must roll back within five minutes while old readers remain active. Should the rule evaluator and persistence/audit owner be split?

feedback.details: The reservation owner atomically enforces no overlap. A separately scaled availability projection may lag up to 10 seconds, so the UI labels its results as candidates and the final write rechecks the invariant. If the prompt did not establish independent read load or tolerated staleness, the extra projection/service would add cost without evidence.

messages.text: The check and commit can race across service boundaries, allowing overlapping bookings.
Independent authorities can both confirm the same resource range before reconciliation.
A 10-second-stale projection is advisory and cannot serialize competing writes.
This preserves ownership but ignores the stated read scaling need; a bounded-stale projection can scale independently.

feedback.reason: The write invariant requires one transaction owner, while high-volume reads can be isolated if their freshness is explicit. Split the projection, not the conflict check from commit.

options.text: Keep slot availability and overlap enforcement in the transactional booking owner.
Put availability checking in a read service and reservation commit in another service without a shared atomic claim.
Allow each booking service instance to maintain its own authoritative slot ledger and reconcile later.
Treat a fresh-enough read projection as the owner of slot reservation and confirm directly from it.
Keep all high-volume availability reads on the transactional write database to avoid a staleness contract.

questions.prompt: Two booking requests can overlap for one resource, and slot ownership is stored in one transactional database. Read availability is high volume and can tolerate 10 seconds of staleness. Which service boundary preserves correctness while scaling reads?

feedback.details: The source writer commits authoritative changes and places durable change data in a replayable stream/log. The index service can scale independently, rebuild from that history, and expose applied watermark/lag up to the 15-second target. Queries must not interpret index lag as source deletion. A projection boundary is appropriate because the source remains authoritative.

messages.text: The projection is allowed to lag and rebuild, so it cannot replace the source of truth.
A service outage would permanently lose updates and prevent the index from catching up.
Temporary projection lag is not evidence of deletion.
The split does not provide independent scaling if its bottleneck remains shared.

feedback.reason: The index has independent scaling and rebuild needs, while its accepted lag means it is a derived projection. Separate it from source ownership and make replay/freshness observable.

options.text: Run indexing as a separate projection with its own write/query budgets and explicit lag.
Move authoritative record writes to the search index and infer source state from indexed documents.
Create a separate index service that receives best-effort updates with no durable change log or replay path.
Treat records absent from the current index as deleted in the source service.
Separate source and index deployments but route both through the same exhausted indexing worker pool.

questions.prompt: Search indexing has independent CPU and storage growth from source writes. Analysts can tolerate up to 15 seconds of index lag, and the index must be rebuildable by replaying source changes. How should service ownership be split?

feedback.details: Keep urgent ingress on a protected short path with reserved capacity. Persist batch plan jobs under one owner and execute them in a separate cost-limited worker pool. Share route data through an explicit versioned contract and ensure planner saturation cannot consume urgent resources. A separate process alone is insufficient if CPU or downstream capacity remains shared.

messages.text: A process/service boundary does not isolate a shared saturated resource.
The urgent 100 ms path becomes dependent on minutes-long computations.
Divergent route authorities can send dispatch using stale or conflicting plans.
Independent scaling does not remove capacity limits; unbounded work can still exhaust planner resources and downstream dependencies.

feedback.reason: The prompt establishes different CPU and latency profiles, so worker isolation is justified. Durable job ownership and budgets are still needed to make the boundary recoverable and bounded.

options.text: Isolate bursty batch planning from urgent dispatch while keeping a reserved urgent lane.
Deploy a separate planner service but let it consume the same CPU and worker pool as urgent dispatch.
Route urgent dispatch through the durable planner queue and wait behind batch work.
Let planner and dispatcher maintain separate authoritative route versions and reconcile after dispatch.
Separate planner workers but accept unlimited expensive jobs into them.

questions.prompt: Route planning consumes bursty CPU for several minutes; urgent dispatch ingress must meet a 100 ms deadline and should remain available during planner saturation. The planner can use durable jobs. Which boundary reduces contention?

feedback.details: Payment service owns one intent bound to amount/parameters and its pending/unknown/final state. An adapter may isolate provider credentials, concurrency, and outage policy, but receives that same intent identity and returns a reconcilable result. Checkout never creates a second charge just because adapter status is missing. If independent failure isolation were not needed, the extra service boundary could be unnecessary.

messages.text: Separate identities can cause duplicate provider charges when outcomes are ambiguous.
A timeout can hide a successful charge; missing local status is not proof of provider failure.
The stated independent outage/rate needs are unresolved.
The boundary loses the information needed to retry and reconcile the original charge.

feedback.reason: The provider adapter has an independent failure mode, but payment intent identity and reconciliation must remain authoritative in one owner. A split is safe only when the same identity crosses it.

options.text: Keep payment intent state and reconciliation in one owner; isolate provider-specific calls behind an adapter.
Let both checkout and provider-adapter services create their own charge IDs for one customer intent.
Move status ownership to the provider adapter and let checkout treat missing adapter state as failed.
Keep a shared provider adapter with no rate isolation so one provider outage blocks every payment path.
Separate the adapter and payment service but pass no stable operation identity or reconciliation status between them.

questions.prompt: Payment intent state must survive provider timeouts and be reconciled before a new charge. The provider adapter has its own outage pattern and needs independent rate limits. Where should the service boundary be?

feedback.details: The accountable fraud owner persists the high-risk case and returns accepted only after that write is durable. Analysis workers consume the case by stable ID and update its status. Capacity isolation can protect admission from slow analysis, but the bridge must retain acceptance proof and provide replay/recovery. A best-effort handoff does not meet the promise.

messages.text: A message loss after the ACK makes the high-risk case disappear.
The caller was promised acceptance before an accountable owner persisted the case.
Separate identities can create duplicate reviews or make one case untraceable.
The slow analysis workload can block the time-sensitive admission path.

feedback.reason: Durable admission is the promise made to the caller; analysis may scale independently only after that promise is recorded under a stable case identity.

options.text: Own durable high-risk admission separately from scalable evidence analysis, with acknowledgment after persistence.
Return accepted from the gateway and send the case to analysis through a best-effort message.
Let slow analysis workers decide whether the original admission succeeded after the caller has already received success.
Have gateway and analysis services independently create case identities and retry missing cases.
Keep durable admission and slow analysis in one saturated worker pool, so analysis delays acceptance.

questions.prompt: High-risk fraud admission must be durable before the caller receives accepted. Slow evidence analysis can scale separately and may finish later. Which ownership boundary preserves accountability?

feedback.details: The export owner records period, snapshot cutoff, rules revision, and exportId before accepting work. Render workers may scale/retry separately, but they consume those immutable inputs and publish one completed artifact for that ID. Later corrections create a new export identity. A service split without pinned inputs makes retries nondeterministic.

messages.text: The same identity can produce different bytes after a correction, breaking audit reproducibility.
The worker cannot reproduce the accepted export because its inputs are not pinned.
Heavy computation can starve interactive traffic despite having an async boundary.
Multiple completion authorities can race and overwrite the canonical output.

feedback.reason: Compute load can scale independently, but artifact meaning depends on one pinned export identity and input snapshot. Keep that state under one owner and let workers render from it.

options.text: Own immutable export identity and snapshot rules with payroll; scale rendering workers behind the job boundary.
Let each worker reread current payroll data when a retry starts and overwrite the artifact for the same export ID.
Move rendering to a separate service but pass only a period, with no source cutoff or rules revision.
Run minute-long export rendering in the same request workers that serve payroll reads and writes.
Let the request service and renderer each decide export completion and publish whichever artifact finishes last.

questions.prompt: Payroll export requests can be accepted quickly, while rendering takes minutes. A retry must return the same bytes for the same period and rules revision; compute workers need independent scaling. Which service boundary is appropriate?

feedback.details: The report owner selects an immutable cutoff/snapshot and binds all aggregate reads to it. Projections may be separated for load if they can serve that version and report their applied watermark within the 10-second freshness contract. Do not combine independently latest values as one report. If a projection cannot prove the cutoff, use the authoritative source or report unavailable/stale.

messages.text: Different cutoffs can yield a total that never existed at one point in time.
The caller cannot tell whether the report uses a coherent cutoff or exceeds the freshness allowance.
Independent cutoffs can drift and cannot guarantee one internally consistent report.
This avoids projection lag but ignores the established read scaling/freshness contract.

feedback.reason: The report cutoff must be shared even if read projections scale independently. One snapshot identity anchors the calculation; watermarks make tolerated lag visible.

options.text: Build reports as a bounded read projection over source-owned aggregates at one declared cutoff.
Let each reporting service read its own latest table state and combine results under one report ID.
Scale projections separately but discard source version and watermark to simplify the API.
